If the lessee has made improvements or constructions that increase the value of the land, they cannot destroy them, nor claim any compensation in this regard.

###### Article 762

The lessee is responsible for all contributions and charges on the property.

With regard to constructions existing at the time of the lease and those that will have been erected in performance of the agreement, they are responsible for repairs of all kinds; but they are not obliged to rebuild the buildings, if they prove that they were destroyed by fortuitous event, by force majeure, or that they perished due to a defect in construction prior to the lease.

They are liable for fire, in accordance with Article 1394, paragraphs 2 and 3, of this code.

###### Article 763

The emphyteuta may acquire for the benefit of the land active easements, and encumber it, by deed, with passive easements for a time that shall not exceed the duration of the lease and subject to notifying the owner.

###### Article 764

The emphyteuta benefits from the right of accession during the duration of the emphyteusis.

###### Article 765

In case of expropriation for public utility, the lessor must make known the right of the emphyteuta, in accordance with the legal provisions in force. Separate compensations are granted to the lessor and to the lessee.

###### Article 766

The lessee alone has the rights to hunt and fish and exercises with regard to mines, mineral deposits, quarries and peat bogs all the rights of the usufructuary.

###### Article 767

The constitutive act of emphyteusis is subject only to the registration and transcription fees established for rental leases of limited duration.

Transfers of any kind having as their object either the right of the lessor or the right of the lessee are subject to the legal provisions concerning transfers of ownership of immovable property. The fee is calculated on the market value determined by an estimated declaration of the parties.

##### Chapitre V : Du droit de superficie

###### Article 768

A piece of land may be subject to a division aimed at conferring on a third party ownership of a part of this land located above or below a conventionally fixed limit. The ownership of the upper part is called superficiary ownership or right of superficies, that of the lower part subsurface ownership. Thus, the right of superficies consists, for the holder of this right, in the fact of possessing constructions, works or plantations on land belonging to another. For the holder of the ownership right on the soil, the right of superficies is a renunciation of accession.

The holder of the right of superficies may encumber with easements the properties that are the object of their right, but only within the limit imposed for the exercise of this right.

###### Article 769

A piece of land may also be subject to a spatial division creating volumes. To each volume corresponds a complete right of ownership.

A descriptive statement of division must obligatorily be executed by notarial deed.

#### Title IV: Servitudes or land services

###### Article 770

A servitude is a charge which encumbers a piece of land for the use and benefit of a piece of land belonging to another owner.

It establishes neither preeminence of one piece of land over the other nor personal obligations for the benefit or at the expense of the owners, but only relationships between the servient land and the dominant land and the services attached to them.

It derives either from the natural situation of the places, or from obligations imposed by law, or from agreements between the owners.

Chapter I: Servitudes which derive from the situation of the places

###### Article 771

Lower lands are subject towards those which are higher to receive the waters which flow naturally from them without the hand of man having contributed to it.

The lower owner cannot erect a dike which prevents this flow.

The upper owner cannot do anything which aggravates the servitude of the lower land.

###### Article 772

Every owner has the right to use and dispose of rainwater which falls on his land. If the use of this water or the direction given to it aggravates the natural servitude of flow established by Article 771, compensation is due to the owner of the lower land.

The same provision is applicable to spring waters arising on a piece of land.

When, through borings or underground works, an owner causes waters to emerge on his land, the owners of the lower lands must receive them; but they are entitled to compensation in case of damage resulting from their flow.

Houses, courtyards, gardens, parks and enclosures adjoining dwellings cannot be subject to any aggravation of the servitude of flow in the cases provided for by the preceding paragraphs.

Disputes which may arise from the establishment and exercise of the servitudes provided for by these paragraphs and the settlement, if applicable, of compensation due to the owners of the lower lands are brought, in first instance, before the judge of the district court of the canton who, in ruling, must reconcile the interests of agriculture and industry with the respect due to property. If expert assessment is required, only one expert may be appointed.

###### Article 773

He who has a spring on his land may always use the waters at his will within the limits and for the needs of his land.

The owner of a spring may no longer use it to the prejudice of the owners of the lower lands who, for more than thirty years, have made and completed, on the land where the spring gushes forth, apparent and permanent works intended to use the waters or to facilitate their passage into their property.

He cannot use it either in a manner to deprive the inhabitants of a municipality, village or hamlet, of the water which is necessary to them; but if the inhabitants have not acquired or prescribed the use thereof, the owner may claim compensation, which is settled by experts.

If, from the exit of the land where they emerge, the spring waters form a watercourse offering the character of public and running waters, the owner cannot divert them from their natural course to the prejudice of the lower users.

###### Article 774

Every owner may compel his neighbor to the demarcation of their contiguous properties.

The demarcation is the operation which allows to recognize and fix, in an adversarial and definitive manner, the separating boundaries of private properties belonging or destined to belong to different owners.

The demarcation is carried out by common agreement of the parties and, failing that, by a decision of the judge seized by one of them or, within the framework of the registration procedure of the property, by the sworn surveyor of the Cadastre section who has been designated by the Registrar to carry out the demarcation of the property to be registered.

The demarcation is done at common expense.

###### Article 775

The action for demarcation is perpetual

###### Article 776

Every owner may enclose his land, except for the exception relating to the right of passage set forth in articles794 et seq.

##### Chapter II: Servitudes established by law

###### Article 777

Servitudes established by law are governed by the rules which institute them.

###### Section I: Party wall ownership

###### Article 778

Party wall ownership is an undivided property right over a wall, a fence or a ditch.

###### Article 779

A wall, a fence or a ditch may only be constructed straddling the separating line of two contiguous pieces of land by common agreement of the owners of said lands.

The one of the two who has not consented to this construction cannot, in the urbanized areas of the country, demand the demolition of the wall. He acquires by operation of law and free of charge the party wall ownership thereof.

###### Article 780

Existing walls, fences or a ditch, constructed at the separating boundary or on the line separating two pieces of land, are presumed to be party structures, except for title or contrary factual element.

###### Article 781

Except for contrary title:

- a wall is deemed to belong to the sole owner of the land towards which its top is inclined in its entirety or on the side of which there exist architectural elements attesting to the initial intent of the builders of the wall;
- a ditch is deemed to belong to the sole owner of the land on the side of which the earth thrown up is located;
- a fence is deemed to belong to the sole owner of the enclosed land if only one of the lands is enclosed.

###### Article 782

The costs of repair and reconstruction of a party wall, fence or ditch are apportioned between the owners in proportion to the rights of each, unless the costs have been made necessary by the act of one of them. The latter must then bear the entire cost. However, any owner of a party wall, fence or ditch, may exempt himself from these costs, by abandoning his right of party wall ownership, unless the wall supports a building belonging to him or the ditch serves for the flow of waters from his land.

###### Article 783

Each of the owners may support his construction on the party wall.

###### Article 784

Any co-owner may have the party wall raised; but he must alone pay the cost relating both to the raising and to future maintenance repairs above the current height of the common enclosure.

If the party wall is not in a condition to support the raising, he who nevertheless intends to raise it must have the wall entirely rebuilt at his expense, and any excess thickness which may be necessary must be taken from his side.

The neighbor who has not contributed to the raising may acquire party wall ownership thereof by paying half of the cost it incurred and the value of half of the ground provided for the excess thickness, if there is

a. The cost which the raising incurred is estimated at the date of acquisition, taking into account the condition in which the raised part of the wall is found.

###### Article 785

Any owner adjoining a wall has the option to make it a party wall in whole or in part, by reimbursing to the owner of the wall half of the current value of the wall and half of the value of the ground supporting the wall or the part of the wall.

This option does not apply to other types of enclosure nor to ditches.

###### Article 786

No owner may carry out works affecting or likely to affect the structure of the party wall, fence or ditch without the consent of the other or, failing that, the authorization of the judge.

###### Article 787

The fruits and products of a party hedge belong to the owners in equal shares.

The co-owner of a party hedge may destroy it up to the boundary of his property, provided that he builds a wall on that boundary. The same rule applies to the co-owner of a party ditch that serves only as an enclosure.

The trees that are in the party hedge are party trees like the hedge. Each owner may require the uprooting or pruning of a party tree as soon as it is isolated and does not form part of the enclosure.

###### Section II: Distances to be observed between neighboring lands

###### Article 788

Anyone who builds on his land is obliged to observe the distance prescribed by the regulations and particular customs according to the works in question.

###### Article 789

Similarly, the planting of vegetation is governed by administrative regulations or by constant and recognized customs. In the absence thereof and subject to particular provisions on urban planning, it is permitted to have trees, shrubs and bushes near the boundary of the neighboring property only at a distance of two meters from the dividing line of the two lands for plantations whose height exceeds two meters, and at a distance of half a meter for other plantations.

###### Article 790

The neighbor may require that trees, shrubs and bushes planted at a lesser distance or whose branches extend over his land be uprooted or reduced to the legal height or distance. He may also cut himself what overhangs his land, provided that this does not cause the plant in question to die, failing which he will be liable for it.

If it is the roots, brambles or twigs that extend over his land, he has the right to cut them himself at the boundary of the dividing line. This right is imprescriptible.

The fruits that have fallen naturally from these branches belong to him.

###### Article 791

Jours are openings or fixtures that allow a view towards the neighbor's land, such as a window, a balcony or a platform.

Vues are openings or fixtures that allow air or light to pass through, but that do not allow a view towards the neighbor's land, such as a translucent brick.

Jours and vues constitute external fixtures within the meaning of the provisions relating to easements. Therefore:

- no opening, neither jour nor vue, is permitted when the wall is party, unless all the owners agree;
- only jours are permitted when the wall is private and is built on the dividing boundary of the neighboring land;
- when the wall is built by the owner of a land at a distance from the dividing line of the lands, any direct view must be at 1.90 meters from that boundary; and any oblique view must be at 0.60 meters from that same boundary. This distance is calculated from the center of the opening to the dividing boundary of the lands.

###### Article 792

The distance rules provided for in the preceding article do not apply to openings that face an area belonging to the public domain, nor when particular provisions on urban planning provide for other rules.

They do not apply either when the contemplated opening faces a land subject to an easement that prevents constructions, such as a right of way easement, established for the benefit of the person who wants to open the view, provided that the distance between the contemplated opening and the boundary of exercise of the easement in the neighboring land is at least three meters.

###### Section III: Drainage from roofs

###### Article 793

Every owner must construct his roofs so that rainwater flows onto his land or onto the public way; he may not cause it to discharge onto his neighbor's land.

###### Section IV: Right of way

###### Article 794

The owner whose lands are landlocked may claim a sufficient right of way over the lands of his neighbors, subject to compensation proportionate to the damage he may cause, unless the state of being landlocked was voluntarily created.

A land is landlocked if it has no access to the public way, or only insufficient access, to allow its normal use or agricultural, industrial or commercial exploitation.

###### Article 795

The right of way must normally be taken on the side where the route is the shortest from the landlocked land to the public way, unless another route is less damaging, in which case that route must be preferred.

###### Article 796

If the landlocking results from the division of a land following a sale, an exchange, a partition or any other contract, the right of way may only be claimed over the lands that were the subject of these acts. However, in the case where a sufficient right of way could not be established over the divided lands, article 794 would be applicable.

###### Article 797

The action for compensation, in the case provided for by article 794, is subject to prescription, and the right of way may be continued, even though the action for compensation is no longer admissible.

The maintenance of the right of way is the responsibility of the owner of the dominant estate, unless otherwise agreed.

###### Article 798

In case of cessation of the landlocking and regardless of the manner in which the site and mode of the easement were determined, the owner of the servient estate may, at any time, invoke the extinction of the easement.

In the absence of an amicable agreement, this termination is established by a judicial decision.

##### Chapitre III: Easements established by act of man

###### Section I: The various kinds of easements that may be established on property

###### Article 799

Easements are either continuous or discontinuous.

Continuous easements are those whose use is or can be continual without requiring the actual act of man: such are water pipes, drains, views and others of this kind. Discontinuous easements are those that require the actual act of man to be exercised: such are rights of way, drawing water, pasturing and other similar rights.

###### Article 800

Easements are apparent or non-apparent.

Apparent easements are those that are indicated by external works, such as a door, a window, an aqueduct.

Non-apparent easements are those that have no external sign of their existence, such as, for example, the prohibition to build on a land, or to build only to a specified height.

###### Section II: How easements are established

###### Article 801

Easements that do not result from the configuration of the places or that are imposed by law can only be acquired by title.

By way of exception, continuous and apparent easements may be established by destination of the father of the family: There is destination of the father of the family when, in the absence of a provision to the contrary in the act of division, it is proven that the two lands currently divided belonged to the same owner, and that the works or external fixtures from which the easement results were made by him before the division of the land and have been maintained since.

###### Article 802

If the owner of two lands between which there exists an apparent sign of an easement disposes of one of the lands without the contract containing any agreement relating to the easement, it continues to exist actively or passively in favor of the alienated land or on the alienated land.

###### Article 803

When an easement is established, one is deemed to grant everything that is necessary to use it. Thus the easement to draw water from another's fountain necessarily entails the right of way.

###### Section III: Rights of the owner of the land to which the easement is due

###### Article 804

The person to whom an easement is due has the right to make all works necessary to use it and to preserve it.

###### Article 805

These works are at his expense, and not at that of the owner of the servient land, unless the deed establishing the servitude provides otherwise.

###### Article 806

Even in the case where the owner of the servient land is charged by the deed to carry out at his expense the works necessary for the use or conservation of the servitude, he may always free himself from the charge by abandoning the servient land to the owner of the land to which the servitude is owed.

###### Article 807

If the land for which the servitude was established comes to be divided, the servitude remains owed for each portion, without however the condition of the servient land being aggravated.

Thus, for example, if it concerns a right of way, all the co-owners shall be obliged to exercise it through the same place.

###### Article 808

The owner of the land subject to the servitude may not do anything that tends to diminish its use or to make it more inconvenient.

Thus, he may not change the state of the premises, nor transfer the exercise of the servitude to a place different from that where it was originally assigned.

But however, if this original assignment had become more onerous to the owner of the servient land, or if it prevented him from making advantageous repairs thereto, he could offer to the owner of the other land a place equally convenient for the exercise of his rights, and the latter could not refuse it.

###### Article 809

For his part, he who has a right of servitude may only use it according to his title, without being able to make, either in the land which owes the servitude or in the land to which it is owed, any change that aggravates the condition of the former.

###### Section IV: How servitudes are extinguished

###### Article 810

Servitudes cease when things are in such a state that they can no longer be used.

They revive if things are restored in such a manner that they can be used.

###### Article 811

Any servitude is extinguished when the land to which it is owed and the one which owes it are united in the same hand.

###### Article 812

The servitude is extinguished by non-use for thirty years, unless it is registered in the Land Register. The period begins to run from the day on which the holder of the dominant land ceased to enjoy it, in the case of discontinuous servitudes, and from the day on which an act contrary to the servitude was performed, in the case of continuous servitudes.

###### Article 813

If the land in favour of which the servitude is established belongs to several persons in undivided ownership, the enjoyment by one prevents extinctive prescription with regard to all.

If, among the co-owners, there is one against whom prescription could not run, such as a minor, he shall have preserved the right of all the others.

## BOOK III. THE DIFFERENT WAYS IN WHICH PROPERTY IS ACQUIRED

General Provisions

###### Article 814

Ownership of property is acquired and transferred by succession, by inter vivos or testamentary donation, by the effect of obligations, by accession or incorporation, by occupation, by delivery, by prescription, or any other mode of acquisition provided by law.

Title I: Successions

Chapter I: The opening of successions and the seisin of heirs

###### Article 815

Successions open, upon death, at the last domicile of the deceased.

They are devolved, when the deceased has not disposed of his property by gifts or will, according to the present provisions of the civil code whenever the spouses have opted for the civil code regime upon their marriage or an unmarried person has expressed his will to that effect with the civil status officer. Gifts and wills are authorized to the extent compatible with the reserved portion.

The provisions of this title apply to the succession of a person subject to bankruptcy proceedings, subject to the special provisions provided in this area.

###### Article 816

Agreements which have the object of creating rights or renouncing rights over all or part of a succession not yet opened or of property dependent thereon produce effect only in cases where they are authorized by law.

###### Article 817

The law regulates the order of succession among the various heirs and the surviving spouse.

Universal legatees and donees are seised under the conditions provided in title II, Inter vivos donations and wills, of this book.

Failing them, the succession is acquired by the State.

###### Article 818

The heirs and the surviving spouse are seised by operation of law of the property, rights and actions of the deceased, subject to the obligation to discharge all the charges of the succession.

The State must have itself sent into possession.

###### Article 819

The provisions of this title, particularly those concerning undivided ownership and partition, apply mutatis mutandis to universal legatees and donees or legatees and donees by universal title, when not derogated by a particular rule.

##### Chapter II: The qualifications required to succeed - Proof of the quality of heir

###### Section I: The qualifications required to succeed

###### Article 820

To succeed, one must necessarily exist at the moment of the opening of the succession or, having already been conceived, be born viable.

A person whose absence is presumed within the meaning of articles 142 and following may succeed.

###### Article 821

When several persons who had a right to succeed one another perish in the same event, the order of deaths is established by all means.

Persons who die without it being possible to establish which survived the other are deemed to have died at the same instant, if at least one of them is called to the succession of the other. The succession of each of them is then devolved to the persons who would have been called to receive it in their default.

###### Article 822

Are unworthy to succeed, and, as such, excluded from successions:

1° A person who is convicted of having, alone or with others, voluntarily caused or attempted to cause the death of the deceased;

2° A person who is convicted of having, alone or with others, voluntarily inflicted blows or violence having resulted in the death of the deceased, without intention to cause it;

3° A person who is convicted of having voluntarily refrained from preventing the commission of an offense against the bodily integrity of the deceased from which death resulted, when he could have done so without risk to himself or to third parties;

4° A person who, in criminal proceedings, made against the deceased an accusation or testimony judged false or defamatory;

5° An heir of full age who, having knowledge of the murder of the deceased, did not report it to the authorities. However, the failure to report cannot be invoked against the ascendants and descendants of the murderer, nor against his relatives in the same degree, nor against his husband or his wife, nor against his brothers or sisters, nor against his uncles and aunts, nor against nephews and nieces.

###### Article 823

When by reason of their death, the public action could not be exercised to its conclusion against the persons who committed the acts mentioned in 1° and 2°, these persons may nevertheless be declared unworthy by the court at the request of any heir and, failing that, of the public prosecutor. The request must be made within six months of the death.

###### Article 824

When the deceased, subsequent to the facts which constitute the cause of unworthiness, had knowledge thereof and specified, in an express manner and in testamentary form, that he intended to maintain the heir in his rights or made him a universal gift or a gift by universal title, this successor affected by a cause of unworthiness is not excluded from the succession.

###### Article 825

The heir excluded from the succession on grounds of unworthiness is required to return all the fruits and all the revenues which he has enjoyed since the opening of the succession.

###### Article 826

The children of the unworthy person are not excluded by the fault of their ancestor, whether they come to the succession in their own right, or by effect of representation; but the unworthy person may not, in any case, claim, on the property of this succession, the usufruct that the law grants to fathers and mothers on the property of their children.

###### Section II: Proof of the quality of heir

###### Article 827

Proof of the quality of heir is established by all means.

This does not derogate from the customs concerning the issuance of certificates of ownership or inheritance by judicial or administrative authorities.

###### Article 828

Proof of the quality of heir may result from a certificate of notoriety drawn up by a notary, at the request of one or more beneficiaries.

The certificate of notoriety must refer to the death certificate of the person whose succession is open and mention the supporting documents that could be produced, such as civil status records and, where applicable, documents concerning the existence of liberalities upon death that may have an impact on the succession devolution.

It contains the affirmation, signed by the beneficiary or beneficiaries who are the authors of the request, that they have a claim, alone or with others whom they designate, to collect all or part of the succession of the deceased.

Any person whose statements would appear useful may be called to the act.

Mention is made of the existence of the certificate of notoriety in the margin of the death certificate.

###### Article 829

The certificate of notoriety thus established has evidentiary value until proof to the contrary.

The person who relies on it is presumed to have hereditary rights in the proportion indicated therein, and the heirs designated in the certificate of notoriety or their common representative are deemed, with regard to third parties holding property of the succession, to have free disposal of such property and, in the case of funds, free disposal thereof in the proportion indicated in the certificate.

The certificate of notoriety does not, by itself, entail acceptance of the succession.

###### Article 830

Anyone who, knowingly and in bad faith, relies on an inaccurate certificate of notoriety, incurs the sanctions provided for in Article 888, without prejudice to damages.

##### Chapitre III: Order of successions

###### Article 831

Successions devolve to the relatives and to the successible spouse of the deceased, in the order and according to the rules determined below.

The successible spouse is the surviving spouse who is not divorced.

###### Section I: Rights of relatives in the absence of a successible spouse

###### § 1. General provisions

###### Article 832

The law does not distinguish according to the modes of establishment of filiation to regulate succession. The rights resulting from adoptive filiation are regulated in Title IX of this code, relating to adoption under the Civil Code.

###### Article 833

In the absence of a successible spouse, relatives are called to succeed as follows: 1° Children and their descendants;

2° Father and mother; brothers and sisters and the descendants of the latter;

3° Ascendants other than father and mother;

4° Collaterals other than brothers and sisters and the descendants of the latter. Each of these four categories constitutes an order of heirs which excludes the following ones.

###### Article 834

Children or their descendants succeed to their father and mother or other ascendants, without distinction of sex or primogeniture, even if they are born of different unions.

###### Article 835

When the deceased leaves neither issue, nor brother, nor sister, nor descendants of the latter, his father and mother succeed to him, each for half.

###### Article 836

When the father and mother died before the deceased and the latter leaves no issue, the brothers and sisters of the deceased or their descendants succeed to him, to the exclusion of other relatives, ascendants or collaterals.

###### Article 837

When the father and mother survive the deceased and the latter has no issue, but has brothers and sisters or descendants of the latter, the succession devolves, for one quarter, to each of the father and mother and, for the remaining half, to the brothers and sisters or their descendants.

When only one of the father and mother survives, the succession devolves for one quarter to the latter and for three quarters to the brothers and sisters or their descendants.

###### Article 838

When only the father or the mother survives and the deceased has neither issue nor brother nor sister nor descendant of the latter, but leaves one or more ascendants of the other branch than that of his surviving father or mother, the succession devolves for half to the father or mother and for half to the ascendants of the other branch.

###### Article 839

When the father and mother or one of them survives the deceased and the latter has no issue, they may in all cases exercise a right of return, up to the shares fixed in the first paragraph of Article 837, on the property that the deceased had received from them by donation.

The value of the portion of property subject to the right of return is credited primarily against the succession rights of the father and mother.

When the right of return cannot be exercised in kind, it is executed in value, within the limit of the succession assets.

###### Article 840

In the absence of an heir of the first two orders, the succession devolves to ascendants other than father and mother.

###### Article 841

In the absence of an heir of the first three orders, the succession devolves to the collateral relatives of the deceased other than brothers and sisters and the descendants of the latter.

###### § 2. Degrees and branches

###### Article 842

The proximity of kinship is established by the number of generations; each generation is called a degree.

###### Article 843

The sequence of degrees forms the line. The direct line is the sequence of degrees between persons who descend from one another, and the collateral line is the sequence of degrees between persons who do not descend from one another but who descend from a common ancestor.

The direct line is distinguished into descending direct line and ascending direct line. The first is that which links the head with those who descend from him; the second is that which links a person with those from whom he descends.

###### Article 844

In the direct line, there are as many degrees as there are generations between persons. Thus, the child is, in relation to the father and mother, in the first degree; the grandson or granddaughter in the second; and reciprocally from the father and mother in relation to the child and from the grandparents in relation to the grandson or granddaughter; and so on.

In the collateral line, the degrees are counted by generation, from one of the relatives up to but not including the common ancestor, and from the latter to the other relative. Thus, brothers and sisters are in the second degree; the uncle or aunt and the nephew or niece are in the third degree; first cousins in the fourth degree; and so on.

###### Article 845

In each order, the nearest heir excludes the more distant heir in degree. At equal degree, heirs succeed in equal portions and per capita.

All of the above subject to what will be said below regarding division by branches and representation.

###### Article 846

Collateral relatives belonging to the order of heirs mentioned in 4° of Article 833 do not succeed beyond the sixth degree.

###### Article 847

Kinship is divided into two branches, depending on whether it proceeds from the father or the mother.

When the succession devolves to ascendants, it is divided in half between those of the paternal branch and those of the maternal branch.

###### Article 848

In each branch succeeds, to the exclusion of all others, the ascendant who is in the closest degree.

Ascendants in the same degree succeed per capita.

In the absence of an ascendant in one branch, the ascendants of the other branch take the entire succession.

###### Article 849

When the succession devolves to collaterals other than brothers and sisters or their descendants, it is divided in half between those of the paternal branch and those of the maternal branch.

###### Article 850

In each branch succeeds, to the exclusion of all others, the collateral who is in the closest degree.

Collaterals in the same degree succeed per capita.

In the absence of a collateral in one branch, the collaterals of the other branch take the entire succession.

###### § 3. De la représentation

###### Article 851

Representation is a legal fiction, the effect of which is to call to the succession the representatives, in the place, in the degree and in the rights of the person represented.

###### Article 852

Representation takes place ad infinitum in the direct descending line.

It is allowed in all cases, whether the children of the deceased compete with the descendants of a predeceased child, or whether all the children of the deceased having died before him, the descendants of said children find themselves among themselves in equal or unequal degrees.

###### Article 853

Representation does not take place in favor of ascendants; the closest, in each of the two lines, always excludes the more remote.

###### Article 854

In the collateral line, representation is allowed in favor of children and descendants of brothers or sisters of the deceased, whether they come to his succession concurrently with uncles or aunts, or whether all the brothers and sisters of the deceased having predeceased, the succession is devolved to their descendants in equal or unequal degrees.

###### Article 855

In all cases where representation is allowed, the division is made by stirpes, as if the person represented were coming to the succession: if the same stirps has produced several branches, the subdivision is also made by stirpes in each branch. Within a stirps or subdivision of a stirps, the division is made per capita.

###### Article 856

One does not represent living persons, but only those who are dead; one may represent a person whose succession one has renounced.

One represents renunciants only in successions devolved in the direct or collateral line. The children of the renunciant conceived before the opening of the succession from which the renunciant was excluded bring back to the succession of the latter the property which they inherited in his stead, if they come in competition with other children conceived after the opening of the succession. The collation is made according to the provisions set forth in articles 994 et seq. of this Code.

Unless the donor intends otherwise, in case of representation of a renunciant, the donations made to the latter are imputed, where applicable, to the forced share that should have gone to him had he not renounced. The law does not distinguish, for the exercise of representation, between legitimate filiation and natural filiation.

###### Article 857

Representation is allowed in favor of the children and descendants of an unworthy person, even if the latter is alive at the opening of the succession.

The provisions set forth in the second paragraph of article 856 are applicable to the children of the unworthy person during his lifetime.

###### Section II : Des droits du conjoint survivant

###### § 1. De la nature des droits, de leur montant et de leur exercice

###### Article 858

The successor spouse is called to the succession, either alone or in competition with the relatives of the deceased.

###### Article 859

If the predeceased spouse leaves children or descendants, the surviving spouse takes, at his or her choice, the usufruct of all the existing property or ownership of one quarter of the property when all the children are issue of both spouses and ownership of one quarter in the presence of one or more children who are not issue of both spouses.

###### Article 860

If, in the absence of children or descendants, the deceased leaves his father and mother, the surviving spouse takes half of the property. The other half devolves one quarter to the father and one quarter to the mother. When the father or mother has predeceased, the share that would have gone to him or her falls to the surviving spouse.

###### Article 861

In the absence of children or descendants of the deceased and his father and mother, the surviving spouse takes the entire succession.

###### Article 862

By way of derogation from article 861, in case of predeceasing of the father and mother, the property that the deceased had received from his ascendants by succession or donation and which are found in kind in the succession are, in the absence of descendants, devolved for half to the brothers and sisters of the deceased or to their descendants, themselves descendants of the predeceased parent or parents at the origin of the transmission.

###### Article 863

When the surviving spouse takes all or three quarters of the property, the ascendants of the deceased, other than the father and mother, who are in need benefit from a claim for support against the succession of the predeceased.

The period for claiming it is one year from the death or from the moment from which the heirs cease to pay the benefits they previously provided to the ascendants. The period is extended, in case of undivided ownership, until completion of the partition.

The pension is deducted from the succession. It is borne by all the heirs and, in case of insufficiency, by all the specific legatees, proportionally to their emolument. However, if the deceased has expressly declared that such legacy shall be paid in preference to others, article 1080 shall apply.

###### Article 864

When the spouse has the choice of ownership or usufruct, his rights are non-transferable as long as he has not exercised his option.

###### Article 865

The spouse's option between usufruct and ownership is proved by any means.

Any heir may invite the spouse in writing to exercise his option. Failing to have taken a position in writing within three months, the spouse is deemed to have opted for the usufruct.

The spouse is deemed to have opted for the usufruct if he dies without having taken a position.

###### Article 866

The calculation of the right in full ownership of the spouse provided for in articles 859 and 860 shall be made on a mass composed of all property existing at the death of his spouse to which shall be notionally added those of which he would have disposed, either by inter vivos act or by testamentary act, for the benefit of successors, without exemption from collation.

The spouse may only exercise his right over property of which the predeceased will not have disposed either by inter vivos act or by testamentary act, and without prejudice to forced heirship rights or rights of return.

###### Article 867

The liberalities received from the deceased by the surviving spouse are imputed to the latter's rights in the succession. When the liberalities thus received are less than the rights defined in articles 859 and 860, the surviving spouse may claim the complement, without ever receiving a portion of the property exceeding the quota defined in article 1228.

###### § 2. De la conversion de l'usufruit

###### Article 868

Any usufruct belonging to the spouse over the property of the predeceased, whether it results from the law, from a will or from a donation of property to come, gives rise to a faculty of conversion into a life annuity, at the request of one of the bare owner heirs or of the successor spouse himself.

The faculty of conversion is not susceptible of renunciation. The co-heirs may not be deprived of it by the will of the predeceased.

###### Article 869

In the absence of agreement between the parties, the request for conversion is submitted to the judge. The request for conversion may be made until the final partition.

If the judge grants the request for conversion, the judge determines the amount of the annuity, the security that must be provided by the debtor co-heirs, as well as the type of indexation appropriate to maintain the initial equivalence of the annuity to the usufruct.

However, the judge cannot order, against the will of the spouse, the conversion of the usufruct relating to the dwelling that he or she occupies as a principal residence, as well as the furniture furnishing it.

###### Article 870

By agreement between the heirs and the spouse, the spouse's usufruct may be converted into capital.

###### Article 871

The conversion of the usufruct is included in the partition operations. It does not produce retroactive effect, unless otherwise stipulated by the parties.

###### § 3. On the right to temporary housing and the life right to housing

###### Article 872

If, at the time of death, the successible spouse actually occupies, as a principal residence, a dwelling belonging to the spouses or entirely dependent on the estate, he or she has by operation of law, for one year, the free enjoyment of this dwelling, as well as the furniture, included in the estate, that furnishes it.

If his or her housing was secured by means of a rental lease or a dwelling belonging in undivided part to the deceased, the rent or the occupancy allowance shall be reimbursed to him or her by the estate during the year, as they are paid.

The rights provided for in this article are deemed direct effects of marriage and not succession rights. This article is a matter of public policy.

###### Article 873

Furthermore, except where the deceased has expressed a contrary intention under the conditions of article 1127, the successible spouse who actually occupied, at the time of death, as a principal residence, a dwelling belonging to the spouses or entirely dependent on the estate, has over this dwelling and the furniture included in the estate that furnishes it, until his or her death, a right of habitation and a right of use. When the dwelling is subject to a rental lease, the successible spouse, if he or she actually occupied the premises as a principal residence at the time of death, benefits from the right of use over the furniture included in the estate furnishing it.

The deprivation of these rights of habitation and use expressed by the deceased under the conditions mentioned in the first paragraph has no impact on the usufruct rights that the spouse receives by virtue of law or a liberality, which continue to be governed by their own rules.

These rights of habitation and use are exercised under the conditions provided for in articles 745 paragraph 3, 747 and 748.

The spouse, the other heirs or any one of them may require that an inventory of the movables and a description of the immovable subject to the rights of use and habitation be drawn up.

By way of derogation from article 745, paragraph 3, when the situation of the spouse is such that the dwelling encumbered with the right of habitation is no longer adapted to his or her needs, the spouse or his or her representative may rent it for purposes other than commercial or agricultural in order to generate the resources necessary for new accommodation conditions.

###### Article 874

The value of the rights of habitation and use is imputed to the value of the succession rights received by the spouse.

If the value of the rights of habitation and use is less than that of his or her succession rights, the spouse may take the balance from the existing property.

If the value of the rights of habitation and use is greater than that of his or her succession rights, the spouse is not required to compensate the estate for the excess.

###### Article 875

The spouse has one year from the death to express his or her intention to benefit from these rights of habitation and use.

The successible spouse and the heirs may, by agreement, convert the rights of habitation and use into a life annuity or into capital.

If there is among the successibles who are parties to the agreement a minor or a protected adult, the agreement must be authorized by the president of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance.

###### § 4. On the right to maintenance

###### Article 876

The estate of the predeceased spouse owes a maintenance allowance to the successible spouse who is in need. The time limit for claiming it is one year from the death or from the time when the heirs cease to pay the benefits they previously provided to the spouse. The time limit is extended, in case of undivided ownership, until the completion of the partition.

The maintenance allowance is taken from the estate. It is borne by all the heirs and, in case of insufficiency, by all the particular legatees, in proportion to their emolument. However, if the deceased has expressly declared that such a legacy shall be paid in preference to others, article 1080 shall apply.

##### Chapter IV. On the rights of the State

###### Article 877

In the absence of heirs, surviving spouse, legatees or universal donees, the estate passes to the State.

The State is required to have seals affixed and, if the inventory of property has not already been carried out within the framework of the procedure provided for under the title of vacant estates, the domain authority shall proceed thereto in the forms prescribed for the acceptance of estates with benefit of inventory.

###### Article 878

It must request the grant of possession from the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance in whose jurisdiction the estate is opened.

The State is exempted from having recourse to the services of a lawyer; the court rules on the request three months and forty days after publication and posting in the customary forms, and after having heard the public prosecutor.

###### Article 879

In the case where the vacancy had been duly declared, and the domain administration appointed curator, it may, before filing its request, proceed itself with the publicity formalities provided for.

###### Article 880

The domain administration that has not fulfilled the formalities prescribed to it may be ordered to pay damages to the heirs, if any come forward.

##### Chapter V: On the option of the heir

###### Section I: General provisions

###### Article 881

Any successible, the heir with regard to the estate as well as the legatee with regard to the legacy that falls to him or her, may:

- either accept it purely and simply,
- or accept it with benefit of inventory, when he or she has a universal or general title vocation,
- or renounce it.

###### Article 882

The option is indivisible. However, the successible who accumulates more than one succession vocation has, for each of them, a separate right of option.

###### Article 883

This option cannot be exercised before the opening of the estate, neither by marriage contract nor with the consent of the person whose estate is in question.

A conditional or term option is null and void.

###### Article 884

The heir of subsequent rank has the same rights as the heir when the latter renounces the estate or is struck with unworthiness, and this, from the day on which he or she became aware of the renunciation or unworthiness. The same applies to the heirs of the person who dies without having exercised the option, from the death of his or her predecessor; these heirs of the person who dies without having exercised the option exercise the option separately, each for his or her share.

###### Article 885

The power to accept or renounce an estate is prescribed after ten years. At the end of this period, the successible is deemed to have renounced the estate. Anyone who claims to have accepted this estate before the expiration of this period must provide proof thereof.

###### Article 886

The subsequent heir of an heir whose acceptance is annulled shall see the ten-year period run against him only from the final decision finding such nullity.

The heir who has left the surviving spouse in enjoyment of the hereditary property shall see the period run against him only from the death of the latter.

The period does not run either against one who legitimately was unaware of the birth of his right, in particular the opening of the succession.

Moreover, as long as the prescription of the right to accept is not acquired against the heirs who have renounced, they have the faculty to still accept the succession, if it has not already been accepted by other heirs; without prejudice however to the rights that may be acquired by third parties over the property of the succession.

###### Article 887

The option exercised has retroactive effect to the day of the opening of the succession.

However, error, fraud as well as violence are a cause of nullity of the option exercised by the heir. The action for nullity is prescribed after five years from the day on which the error or fraud was discovered or from the day on which the violence ceased.

###### Article 888

The heir who, knowingly and in bad faith, has concealed property or rights of a succession, or concealed the existence of a co-heir, or failed to include in the inventory property or rights of the succession, is deprived of the benefit of inventory and of the right of renunciation: he is an unconditional heir, without prejudice to the damages that the victims of his actions could seek. The heir cannot however claim any share in the property or rights misappropriated or concealed. Likewise, when the concealment related to a donation subject to hotchpot or reduction, the heir owes the hotchpot or the reduction of that donation without being able to claim any share in it. The concealing heir is moreover bound to return all the fruits and revenues of the concealed property which he has enjoyed since the opening of the succession.

###### Article 889

The personal creditors of one who refrains from accepting a succession or who renounces a succession to the prejudice of their rights may be authorized in court to accept the succession on behalf of their debtor, in his place and stead.

The acceptance takes place only in favor of these creditors and up to the amount of their claims. It produces no other effect with regard to the heir.

###### Article 890

The acceptance of a succession which would be found to be absorbed or diminished by more than half, by the discovery of a will unknown at the time of acceptance, is voidable for lesion.

###### Section II: Of the acceptance of the succession

###### Article 891

The successions devolved to minors and adults under guardianship may only be validly accepted in accordance with the provisions of the title On Minority, Guardianship and Emancipation.

###### Article 892

The acceptance of the succession may be express or tacit: it is express when the successor takes the title or quality of heir in an authentic or private act; it is tacit when the successor performs an act which necessarily presupposes his intention to accept and which he would only have the right to perform in his quality as heir.

Acts that are purely conservatory, of supervision and of provisional administration are not, in themselves, acts constituting acceptance on the part of the heir. If the successor wishes to perform another act without however taking the title or quality of heir, he must request authorization from the judge to perform it.

###### Article 893

Are deemed purely conservatory:

1° The payment of funeral and last illness expenses, taxes due by the deceased, rents and other succession debts whose settlement is urgent;

2° The collection of fruits and revenues of succession property or the sale of perishable property, subject to justifying that the funds were used to extinguish the debts referred to in 1° or were deposited with a notary or consigned;

3° Any act intended to prevent the aggravation of the succession liabilities;

4° Acts related to the termination of the employment contract of the employee of the deceased private employer, the payment of salaries and compensation due to the employee as well as the delivery of end-of-contract documents.

###### Article 894

Are deemed to be provisional administration:

1° The renewal, as lessor or lessee, of leases which, failing which, would give rise to the payment of compensation;

2° The implementation of administration or disposition decisions initiated by the deceased and necessary for the proper functioning of the enterprise;

3° Acts that are ordinary operations necessary for the continuation, in the short term, of the activity of the enterprise forming part of the succession.

###### Article 895

The heir who, gratuitously or for consideration, transfers his rights in the succession, whether to a stranger, or to all his co-heirs, or to some of them, accepts by that fact alone the succession. The same applies when the heir has renounced the succession, gratuitously or not, in favor of one, several or all of his co-heirs, or in favor of one, several or all heirs of subsequent rank.

###### Article 896

When the person to whom a succession has devolved has died before being able, expressly or tacitly, to express his choice, his heirs may accept it or renounce it on his behalf. In the absence of unanimity among them, the succession must be accepted subject to benefit of inventory.

###### Article 897

When the heir accepts the succession, the effect of the acceptance goes back to the day of the opening of the succession.

###### Section III: Of the renunciation of successions

###### Article 898

The renunciation of a succession is not presumed. It is opposable to all from the day on which it is made at the registry of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the succession was opened, in a special register kept for this purpose.

###### Article 899

The heir who renounces is deemed never to have been an heir.

###### Article 900

The succession to which the heir renounces is distributed among his heirs in direct line; in the absence of heirs in direct line, it passes to the co-heirs and otherwise to the next degree.

The heir who renounces the succession may however retain the gift inter vivos or claim the legacy made to him up to the available portion, unless the donor expressly required hotchpot in case of renunciation. In that case, the hotchpot is made in value; when the value brought in exceeds the rights he should have had in the partition if he had participated in it, the renouncing heir compensates the accepting heirs up to the amount of that excess.

###### Section IV: Of the benefit of inventory

###### § 1. Formalities to be observed

###### Article 901

The declaration of an heir, that he intends to take this quality only subject to benefit of inventory, must be made at the registry of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the succession was opened. It must be recorded in the register intended to receive acts of renunciation.

###### Article 902

The declaration mentions the surname, first names, profession of the heir and the capacity by virtue of which he is called to the succession.

It also includes the election of a single domicile located in Djibouti, which may be the domicile of one of the acceptors subject to benefit of inventory or that of the person in charge of settling the succession. It is to this address that the creditors shall declare their claims.

###### Article 903

The declaration of the heir is registered by the registry, which gives him a receipt for it, and opens a file. The receipt informs the declarant of the necessity to satisfy the publicity provided for by the following article.

###### Article 904

The declaration is published, within fifteen days, in a journal authorized to receive legal publications.

When the law refers to the declaration as the starting point of a time limit, such time limit runs from the date of the publication made.

###### Article 905

The heir's declaration has effect only insofar as it is preceded or followed by a faithful and accurate inventory of the assets of the succession and within the time limits to be determined hereinafter.

###### Article 906

The heir has, first, three months to make an inventory, from the day of the opening of the succession. However, he may request from the judge an additional period if he justifies serious and legitimate reasons that delay the filing of the inventory. In such case, the time limit is suspended from the date of the request for extension.

The heir then has forty days to deliberate on his acceptance or not of the succession. This second time limit begins to run from the day of the expiration of the time limit to which the heir is subject to make the inventory, or from the day of the closing of the inventory if it was completed before the three months.

###### Article 907

The inventory is descriptive and estimative of the elements present, item by item, in the estate of the deceased.

It is drawn up by a bailiff or a notary, according to the rules applicable to these professions.

###### Article 908

A copy of the inventory is delivered against receipt by the heir to the competent registry, which adds it to the file. The heir must carry out this formality within two months of the inventory being made. Failing this, he is deemed to be a pure and simple acceptor of the succession.

###### Article 909

The inventory gives rise to the same publicity as the initial declaration.

Any person who justifies his status as creditor against the deceased may take cognizance of its content and obtain a copy at the registry.

###### § 2. Effects of acceptance subject to inventory benefit

###### Article 910

The declaration made by the heir to accept the succession subject to inventory benefit entails: 1° Separation of estates: the personal assets of the heir are not merged with those of the succession;

2° Preservation of all the rights that the heir had previously over the assets of the deceased; 3° Limitation of the acceptance of the succession to the succession assets: the heir is only required to pay the debts of the succession within the limit of the assets collected and not from his personal estate. The heir can only be held liable for his acts on his personal assets when provisions of this paragraph so provide;

4° Framework for the management of the succession assets by the heir, who is required to administer the succession.

###### Article 911

During the time limits for making an inventory and for deliberating, the heir cannot be compelled to exercise his option. No condemnation can be obtained against him.

As long as the prescription of the right to accept is not acquired against him, the heir may revoke his acceptance and accept the succession purely and simply. He is then deemed to have accepted it from the opening of the succession.

Acceptance subject to inventory benefit prevents any renunciation of the succession.

###### Article 912

If the heir does not file the inventory within the time limits provided for making it, or does not exercise his option within the time limit offered for deliberating, he retains the ability to still make an inventory and to opt. It is otherwise if he has made elsewhere an act manifesting his intention to accept the succession purely and simply or if there exists against him a judgment having become res judicata that condemns him in the capacity of pure and simple heir.

###### Article 913

However, at the expiration of the time limits provided for making an inventory and for deliberating, the heir who has not opted may be summoned, by extrajudicial act, to take a position. The summons may emanate from a creditor of the succession, a co-heir, an heir of subsequent rank, or the State. Within two months following the summons, the heir must take a position or request an additional period from the judge when he has not been able to close the inventory begun or when he justifies other serious and legitimate reasons. This period is suspended from the date of the request for extension until the decision of the judge seized.

Failing to have taken a position at the expiration of the two-month period or the additional period granted, the heir is deemed to be a pure and simple acceptor.

###### Article 914

From the publicity of the declaration of the heir who accepts the succession subject to inventory benefit, the creditors of the succession have a period of twelve months to claim what is due to them. They must declare their claim within this period, by notifying their title to the elected domicile of the succession. In case of late declaration or absence of declaration, claims not secured by securities on the assets of the succession are extinguished with respect to the succession.

This provision also benefits sureties and co-obligors, as well as persons having granted an independent guarantee relating to the claim thus extinguished.

###### Article 915

From the publicity of the declaration of acceptance subject to inventory benefit and for a period of twelve months, it stops or prohibits any enforcement proceeding and any new registration of security by the creditors of the succession, relating to both movables and immovables. However, seizing creditors are considered as holders of securities on the assets and rights previously seized.

###### Article 916

When the succession has been accepted by one or more heirs purely and simply and by one or more others up to the net assets, the rules applicable to this latter option apply to all heirs until the day of partition.

The creditors of a succession accepted by one or more heirs purely and simply and by others up to the net assets may provoke the partition once they justify difficulties in recovering the part of their claim incumbent on the heirs accepting up to the net assets.

###### Article 917

The heir accepting up to the net assets has the obligation to administer the assets he collects in the succession, and must account for his management.

He is liable for serious faults he would commit in this administration.

He must present the account to any succession creditor who requests it and respond within a period of two months to the summons, served by extrajudicial act, to reveal to him where the assets and rights collected in the succession that he has neither alienated nor kept are located. Failing this, he may be constrained on his personal assets.

If he does not wish to personally administer the assets of the succession, or if he is in default, an agent may be appointed in court at the request of any interested party. The President of the Court of First Instance is seized and rules by summary order.

###### Article 918

The heir is owner of the assets of the succession and has the power to dispose of the assets of the succession.

If there are in the succession objects liable to perish or too costly to preserve, the heir may proceed with the sale of these objects. If the heir has decided to keep such assets in kind, at the end of the acceptance procedure subject to inventory benefit, he is only liable for the depreciation or deterioration caused by his negligence.

###### Article 919

For other property, within twelve months from the publication provided for in Article 904, the heir may declare:

1° that he intends to retain in kind certain property of the succession. He then owes to the succession the value of such property as estimated in the inventory;

2° that he sells certain property, movable or immovable.

Such property is excluded from the estate patrimony and removed from the pledge of estate creditors. However, their value is recorded in the assets of the succession. All without prejudice to the rights of creditors with security interests.

Other estate property that has not been the subject of such a declaration remains in the pledge of the creditors of the succession.

###### Article 920

The declaration of the alienation or retention of one or more properties is made within fifteen days to the registry of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance. The heir ensures its publication in a newspaper authorized to receive legal publications.

Without prejudice to the rights reserved to creditors with security interests, any estate creditor may contest before the judge, within three months after the publication mentioned in the first paragraph, the value of the property retained or, when the sale was made amicably, the price of the alienation by proving that the value of the property is higher.

When the creditor's application is granted, the heir is liable for the difference from his personal property, unless he returns to the succession the property retained.

The creditor may also act in his own name to have acts done by his debtor in fraud of his rights declared unenforceable against him, provided that he establishes, in the case of an act for valuable consideration, that the third party co-contractor had knowledge or should have had knowledge of the fraud.

###### Article 921

The declaration to retain property is not enforceable against creditors until it has been published. Failure to declare the alienation of property within the time limit provided for in the preceding article makes the heir liable on his personal property up to the amount of the price of the alienation.

###### Article 922

The heir settles the liabilities of the succession. For this purpose, he draws up a draft settlement of the liabilities. The costs of seals, if any were affixed, of inventory and account, are borne by the succession. The public officer or ministerial officer who settled the succession or allowed the conservation of estate property shall be paid before other creditors.

Registered creditors are paid according to the rank of the security accompanying their claim.

Other creditors who have declared their claim are satisfied in the order of declarations. Legacies of sums of money are delivered after payment of creditors.

###### Article 923

The draft settlement of liabilities is filed with the registry which adds it to the file. A notice is published according to the publication methods provided for in Article 904. Creditors who are not fully satisfied in view of this draft may, within one month of publication, seize the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance in order to contest the draft settlement.

###### Article 924

In the absence of contestation at the end of the one-month period from the publication provided for in the preceding article, the heir must pay the creditors within the following two months, in accordance with the draft settlement of liabilities.

When, conversely, the draft settlement is not validated due to a contestation concerning the order or nature of the claims, the heir deposits the available sums as long as the contestation subsists.

###### Article 925

The personal creditors of the heir may not pursue the recovery of their claims on the property of the succession until the end of the twelve-month period from the publication of the declaration of acceptance of the succession subject to inventory and after the full satisfaction of estate creditors and legatees.

Creditors who have not declared their claim within the time limit referred to in the preceding article, and who come forward only after the exhaustion of the assets, have recourse only against the legatees who have been filled of their rights.

###### Section V: Vacant Successions

###### Article 926

The succession is vacant when, after the expiration of the time limits for making inventory and for deliberating: 1° No one comes forward who claims a succession and there is no known heir; 2° All known heirs have renounced the succession;

3° Known heirs have been summoned to take a position in accordance with the provisions of Article 913 and have renounced the succession or remained silent;

4° In the absence of summons, known heirs have not opted, either expressly or tacitly, for ten years.

When heirs come to make themselves known during the procedure, their hereditary prerogatives take precedence. They may then exercise their legal right of option: if they accept the succession purely and simply, the vacancy automatically ends; if they renounce it, it continues; and if they accept subject to inventory, the procedure continues according to the rules set out in Section IV of this chapter.

###### Article 927

The president of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance in whose jurisdiction the succession is opened, appoints a curator at the request of any interested person or on the requisition of the public prosecutor.

His decision is, at the initiative of the curator, within fifteen days of its pronouncement, published in a newspaper authorized to receive legal announcements.

In the context of vacant successions, the curatorship is necessarily entrusted to the administrative authority in charge of the domain.

###### Article 928

The curator is required, first of all, to have its state established by an inventory: he exercises and pursues its rights; he responds to applications made against the succession; he administers, under the obligation to have the sums of money found in the succession, as well as the amounts from the price of movables or immovables sold, deposited in the National Treasury, for the conservation of rights and under the obligation to account to whom it may concern.

The provisions of Section IV of this chapter, on the forms of inventory, on the mode of administration and on the accounts to be rendered by the beneficiary heir, as well as on the rights and obligations of creditors, are common to curators of vacant successions, subject to the following reservations.

###### Article 929

Creditors must declare their claim to the curator, by notifying him of their title, within nine months.

The curator establishes a draft settlement of liabilities respecting the order provided for in Article 922, the costs related to the administration of the curatorship being paid before other claims. The curator may only provide for the payment of debts of the succession up to the amount of the assets.

The curator may however pay, without waiting for the draft settlement of liabilities, the costs necessary for the conservation of the patrimony, funeral and last illness expenses, taxes owed by the deceased, rents and other estate debts whose settlement is urgent.

###### Article 930

The draft settlement of liabilities is filed with the registry of the Court of First Instance which adds it to the file. A notice is published according to the publication methods provided for in Article 904.

###### Article 931

Creditors who are not fully satisfied according to this draft may, within one month of publication, bring the matter before the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance to contest the settlement draft.

Those who have not declared their claim after submission of the draft may only claim from the remaining assets. In the event the assets are insufficient, they have recourse only against the legatees who have been satisfied in their rights. This recourse is prescribed after one year from the realization of all the remaining assets.

###### Article 932

In the absence of recourse against the draft or after the president's decision has become final, the curator proceeds with the final realization of the remaining assets.

Any balance is handed over upon their request to heirs who come forward, if they are within the time limit to claim the estate.

The Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance within whose jurisdiction the estate is opened, seized by the curator, sends the State into possession of the estate.

##### Chapitre VI. Of partition

###### Section I: Of the legal regime of co-ownership

###### § 1. General provisions

###### Article 933

Co-ownership arises when several persons have a real right of the same nature over the same property or the same mass of properties. This right may be ownership or another divided real right. Co-ownership does not have legal personality.

Each co-owner has over the undivided property the same right shared with the others. The extent of each person's rights in the co-ownership is defined by the law or the agreement that gives rise to it. In the absence of another title, it results from a certificate of notoriety or an inventory heading established by the notary.

###### Article 934

Each co-owner holds their share. However, when a co-owner intends to transfer all or part of their undivided rights, for valuable consideration and to a person outside the co-ownership, the other co-owners have a right of pre-emption.

Any draft transfer must be notified in advance to the other co-owners, with all useful information, such as the price, the conditions of the transfer and the identifying details of the purchaser. This notification, carried out by extra-judicial act, opens a period of one month for the co-owners to bring to the transferring co-owner's knowledge their decision to exercise their right of pre-emption under the conditions brought to their knowledge.

The person who decides to pre-empt has two months to complete the transfer, from the sending of their decision to the transferring co-owner. After this period, they are formally notified to respond and, if they remain silent for fifteen days, their declaration of pre-emption is null and void by operation of law, without prejudice to damages that may be claimed by the transferor.

When the transferor has granted payment terms and, as a result of economic circumstances, the value of the property that has fallen to them has increased or decreased by more than one quarter since the partition, the sums remaining due increase or decrease in the same proportion, unless the parties exclude this variation.

###### Article 935

When a creditor seizes all or part of a co-owner's rights in the co-ownership with a view to subjecting them to a forced sale, there is no right of pre-emption but a right of substitution for the successful bidder. The attorney of the pursuing creditor or the notary informs all the other co-owners one month before the scheduled date of the sale. The latter benefit from a period of one month from the adjudication, to substitute themselves for the purchaser.

This right is exercised by declaration to the registry of the Court of First Instance or to the notary in charge of the sale. It is recorded in the book of conditions of sale established with a view to the sale.

###### Article 936

For both amicable and forced transfers, compliance with the rules of notification and time limits is prescribed on pain of nullity of the transaction. This nullity, of private interest, is available for five years to the persons to whom the notifications should have been made or to their heirs.

The notifications provided for by the two preceding articles and paragraph must be addressed to every bare owner and every usufructuary. But a usufructuary may only acquire a share in bare ownership if no bare owner comes forward as purchaser; a bare owner may only acquire a share in usufruct if no usufructuary comes forward as purchaser.

###### § 2. Of the rules of management of co-ownership

###### Article 937

In co-ownership, decisions are taken unanimously, subject to the following reservations.

###### Article 938

When they fall within the normal operation of the undivided property, decisions concerning the following may be taken by the holders of two-thirds of the undivided rights:

1° Acts of administration of the undivided property;

2° The designation of a co-owner or a third party under a general administration mandate;

3° The conclusion and renewal of leases other than those relating to a building for agricultural, commercial, industrial or artisanal use;

4° The decision to sell undivided movable property when this transaction is necessary for the payment of the debts and charges of the co-ownership. The sale of an undivided property outside this purpose requires unanimity, except with judicial authorization.

###### Article 939

Except in the case of division of ownership of the property or if one of the co-owners is in one of the cases provided for in Article 863, the alienation of an undivided property may be authorized by the Court of First Instance, at the request of one or more co-owners holding at least two-thirds of the undivided rights, according to the conditions and procedures defined in the following paragraphs.

The co-owner or co-owners holding at least two-thirds of the undivided rights express before a notary, by this majority, their intention to proceed with the alienation of the undivided property. In the month following, the notary has this intention served on the other co-owners.

In the absence of opposition within three months of the service, the decision to alienate the undivided property is confirmed, unless the service provided for in the second paragraph has not been carried out. In case of opposition, the Court of First Instance may authorize the alienation of the undivided property if it does not excessively infringe the rights of the other co-owners.

This alienation is carried out by licitation. The sums withdrawn from it cannot be the subject of reinvestment except to pay the debts and charges of the co-ownership.

###### Article 940

Any co-owner may take the measures necessary for the preservation of the undivided property, even if there is no urgency.
