A claim for interest made against one of the joint and several debtors causes interest to run with respect to all.

###### Article 1496

The joint and several debtor pursued by the creditor may raise exceptions that are common to all co-debtors, such as nullity that is not purely personal to that debtor or rescission, and those that are personal to him such as incapacity or a defect of consent affecting his will. He may not raise exceptions that are personal to other co-debtors, such as the granting of a term. However, when an exception personal to another co-debtor extinguishes the divisible share of the latter, notably in case of set-off or remission of debt, he may invoke it to have it deducted from the total of the debt.

###### Article 1497

If the thing due has perished by the fault of one or several of the joint and several debtors or at a date when one or several of the joint and several debtors were in default of performance, the other co-debtors remain bound to pay the price of the thing; but these other co-debtors are not bound to pay damages.

###### Article 1498

When one of the debtors becomes sole heir of the creditor, or when the creditor becomes the sole heir of one of the debtors, confusion only extinguishes the joint and several claim for the part and portion of the debtor or the creditor.

###### Article 1499

The creditor who consents to the division of the debt with regard to one of the co-debtors retains his joint and several action against the others, but subject to the deduction of the share of the debtor whom he has released from solidarity.

###### Article 1500

The creditor who receives separately the share of one of the debtors, without reserving in the receipt solidarity or his rights in general, renounces solidarity only with regard to that debtor. The creditor is not deemed to remit solidarity to the debtor when he receives from him a sum equal to the portion for which he is liable, if the receipt does not state that it is for his share.

The same applies to a simple claim brought against one of the co-debtors for his share, if the latter has not acquiesced to the claim, or if no judgment of condemnation has been entered.

###### Article 1501

The creditor who receives separately and without reservation the portion of one of the co-debtors in the arrears or interest of the debt, loses solidarity only for the arrears or interest due, and not for those to fall due, nor for the capital, unless the divided payment has been continued for ten consecutive years.

###### Article 1502

Among themselves, joint and several co-debtors contribute to the debt only each for his share.

The one who has paid beyond his share has recourse against the others in proportion to their own share.

If one of them is insolvent, his share is distributed, by contribution, among the solvent co-debtors, including the one who made the payment and the one who benefited from a remission of solidarity.

On the other hand, if the debt proceeds from a matter that concerns only one of the joint and several co-debtors, the latter alone is liable for the debt with regard to the others; if he has paid it, he has no recourse against his co-debtors; if they have paid it, they have recourse against him.

###### Article 1503

Joint and several co-debtors are jointly and severally liable for the non-performance of the obligation. The burden ultimately falls on those to whom the non-performance is attributable.

###### § 2. De l'obligation divisible et indivisible

###### Article 1504

An obligation is divisible or indivisible according to whether it has as its object either a thing which in its delivery, or an act which in its performance, is or is not susceptible of division, whether material or intellectual.

###### Article 1505

An obligation is indivisible, although the thing or act which is its object is divisible by its nature, if the relationship under which it is considered in the obligation does not render it susceptible of partial performance.

###### Article 1506

Each of the creditors of an indivisible obligation, by nature or by contract, may demand and receive full payment, subject to accounting to the others; but he cannot alone dispose of the claim nor receive the price instead of the thing.

Each of the debtors of such an obligation is liable for the whole; but he has his recourse in contribution against the others.

The same applies to each of the successors of these creditors and debtors.

##### Chapitre II : Les opérations sur obligations

###### Section I : La cession de créance

###### Article 1507

The assignment of a claim is a contract by which the assigning creditor transfers, for valuable consideration or gratuitously, all or part of his claim against the assigned debtor to a third party called the assignee.

It may relate to one or several present or future claims, determined or determinable. It extends to the accessories of the claim.

The debtor's consent is not required, unless the claim has been stipulated unassignable.

###### Article 1508

The assignment of a claim must be evidenced in writing, on pain of nullity.

###### Article 1509

Between the parties, the transfer of the claim takes effect on the date of the instrument.

It is opposable to third parties from that moment. In case of dispute, the burden of proving the date of the assignment lies with the assignee, who may do so by any means.

However, the transfer of a future claim only takes place on the day of its coming into existence, both between the parties and with regard to third parties.

###### Article 1510

The assignment is not opposable to the debtor, if he has not already consented to it, unless it has been notified to him or he has acknowledged it.

The debtor may raise against the assignee exceptions inherent to the debt, such as payment, prescription, nullity, the exception of non-performance, rescission or set-off of connected debts. He may also raise exceptions arising from his relations with the assignor before the assignment became opposable to him, such as the granting of a term, remission of debt or set-off of non-connected debts.

The assignor and the assignee are jointly and severally liable for all additional costs occasioned by the assignment which the debtor does not have to advance. Unless otherwise agreed, the burden of these costs falls on the assignee.

###### Article 1511

Competition between successive assignees of a claim is resolved in favor of the first in date; he has recourse against the one to whom the debtor would have made a payment.

The date to be taken into consideration is that of each of the assignments, the proof of which may be provided by any means.

###### Article 1512

One who assigns a claim for valuable consideration guarantees the existence of the claim and its accessories, unless the assignee has acquired it at his own risk or he was aware of the uncertain nature of the claim.

He is liable for the solvency of the debtor only when he has undertaken to do so, and up to the amount of the price he may have obtained from the assignment of his claim. Any clause to the contrary is deemed unwritten. When the assignor has guaranteed the solvency of the debtor, this guarantee is only understood to apply to present solvency; it may however extend to solvency at maturity, but on condition that the assignor has expressly specified it.

###### Section II : La novation

###### Article 1513

Novation is a contract which has as its object the substitution for an obligation, which it extinguishes, of a new obligation which it creates.

It may take place by substitution of obligation between the same parties, by change of debtor or by change of creditor.

###### Article 1514

Novation is not presumed; the intent to effect it must clearly result from the instrument.

###### Article 1515

Novation only takes place if the old obligation and the new obligation are both valid, unless its declared object is to substitute a valid undertaking for an undertaking tainted with a defect.

###### Article 1516

Novation by change of debtor may be effected without the participation of the initial debtor.

###### Article 1517

Novation by change of creditor requires the consent of the debtor. The latter may, in advance, accept that the new creditor be designated by the first.

Novation is enforceable against third parties as of the date of the act. In case of dispute regarding the date of novation, the burden of proof lies with the new creditor, who may provide it by any means.

###### Article 1518

Novation by substitution of obligation between the same parties is possible, whatever the difference established between the old and the new obligation.

###### Article 1519

The extinction of the old obligation extends to all its accessories.

By way of exception, the original securities may be reserved for the guarantee of the new obligation with the consent of third-party guarantors.

###### Article 1520

Novation agreed between the creditor and one of the joint and several co-debtors releases the others.

Novation agreed between the creditor and a surety does not release the principal debtor. It releases the other sureties up to the contributory share of the one whose obligation was the subject of the novation.

###### Section III: Delegation

###### Article 1521

Delegation is an operation by which one person, the delegator, obtains from another, the delegate, that the latter expressly binds itself towards a third person, the delegatee, who accepts it as debtor. The delegate may not, unless otherwise stipulated, set up against the delegatee any defense arising from its relations with the delegator or from the relations between the latter and the delegatee.

###### Article 1522

Where the delegator is debtor to the delegatee and the delegatee's intention to discharge the delegator results expressly from the act, delegation operates as novation.

However, the delegator remains liable if it has expressly undertaken to guarantee the future solvency of the delegate or if the latter is subject to debt settlement proceedings at the time of delegation.

###### Article 1523

Where the delegator is debtor to the delegatee but the latter has not discharged it from its debt, delegation gives the delegatee a second debtor.

Payment made by one of the two debtors releases the other, to the corresponding extent.

###### Article 1524

Where the delegator is creditor of the delegate, its claim is extinguished only by the performance of the delegate's obligation towards the delegatee and to the corresponding extent.

Until then, the delegator may demand or receive payment thereof only for the portion that would exceed the delegate's commitment. It recovers its rights only by performing its own obligation towards the delegatee.

Assignment or attachment of the delegator's claim produces effect only under the same limitations. However, if the delegatee has released the delegator, the delegate is itself released with regard to the delegator, up to the amount of its commitment towards the delegatee.

###### Article 1525

The mere indication by the debtor of a person designated to pay in its place entails neither novation nor delegation. The same applies to the mere indication by the creditor of a person designated to receive payment for it.

##### Chapter III: Actions Available to the Creditor

###### Article 1526

The creditor is entitled to performance of the obligation; it may compel the debtor thereto under the conditions provided by law and in particular, by the provisions of the code of civil procedure.

###### Article 1527

Where the debtor's failure to exercise its rights and actions of a patrimonial nature jeopardizes the rights of its creditor, the latter may, by means of the oblique action, exercise them on behalf of its debtor, except for those which are exclusively attached to its person. Rights exclusively attached to the person of the debtor are rights and actions the exercise of which is subject to personal considerations of a moral or family nature.

###### Article 1528

The creditor may also act in its own name, by means of the paulian action, to have acts performed by its debtor in fraud of its rights declared unenforceable against it, provided it establishes, if the act is for valuable consideration, that the third-party co-contractor had knowledge of the fraud. The action is available where the debtor has performed an act of impoverishment aimed at organizing its insolvency or making the creditor's enforcement proceedings more difficult. It is also available when the creditor has a special right over property of the debtor and the latter performs an act which has the effect of infringing that special right.

The claim must be certain on the day the action is brought. The enforceability and liquidity of the claim are not a condition for the paulian action.

###### Article 1529

In cases determined by law, the creditor may bring a direct action for payment of its claim against a debtor of its debtor.

##### Chapter IV: Extinction of the Obligation

###### Section I: Payment

###### Subsection 1: General Provisions

###### Article 1530

Payment is the voluntary performance of the due obligation.

It must be made as soon as the debt becomes enforceable; it may be made even by a person not bound thereto, except in case of legitimate refusal by the creditor.

Payment releases the debtor with regard to the creditor and extinguishes the debt, except where the law or the contract provides for subrogation in the creditor's rights.

###### Article 1531

Payment must be made to the creditor or to the person designated to receive it.

Payment made to a person who was not qualified to receive it is nevertheless valid if the creditor ratifies it or has benefited therefrom.

Payment made to a creditor lacking capacity to contract is not valid, unless the creditor has benefited therefrom.

###### Article 1532

Payment made in good faith to an apparent creditor is valid.

###### Article 1533

The creditor may refuse partial payment even if the performance is divisible. It may accept to receive in payment something other than what is owed to it.

###### Article 1534

The debtor of an obligation to deliver a specific thing is released by its delivery to the creditor in the condition it is in, except for proving, in case of deterioration, that the deterioration is not due to its act or to that of persons for whom it must answer.

If the debt is of a thing determined only by its kind, the debtor shall not be required, in order to be released, to give it of the best kind; but it may not offer it of the worst.

###### Article 1535

In the absence of another designation by law, the contract or the judge, payment must be made at the domicile of the debtor.

###### Article 1536

The costs of payment are, unless otherwise provided by law or clause, borne by the debtor.

###### Article 1537

Payment is proved by any means.

###### Article 1538

Voluntary delivery by the creditor to the debtor of the original under private signature or of the enforceable copy of the title of its claim constitutes a simple presumption of release.

The same delivery to one of the joint and several co-debtors produces the same effect with regard to all.

###### Article 1539

The debtor of several debts may indicate, when it pays, which one it intends to discharge.

In the absence of indication by the debtor, imputation takes place as follows: first to debts that have fallen due; among these, to the debts which the debtor had the greatest interest in discharging. Where interests are equal, imputation is made to the oldest; all things being equal, it is made proportionally.

###### Subsection 2: Special provisions relating to monetary obligations

###### Article 1540

The debtor of a monetary obligation is discharged by payment of its nominal amount. The amount of the sum due may however vary by operation of indexation or debts of value. A debt of value is an obligation that has as its object, not a determined sum of money, but a value that may give rise, depending on the time, to different valuations, such as a debt for damages which is determined on the day of judgment and not on the day of the harmful act. The debtor of a debt of value is discharged by payment of the sum of money resulting from its liquidation.

###### Article 1541

Where the monetary obligation bears interest, the debtor is discharged by paying the principal and interest. Partial payment is imputed first to interest, unless otherwise agreed. Interest is granted by law or stipulated in the contract. The rate of contractual interest must be fixed in writing. It is deemed annual by default.

###### Article 1542

Accrued interest, due for at least one full year, bears interest if the contract so provides or if a judicial decision specifies it.

###### Article 1543

Payment, in Djibouti, of a monetary obligation is made in Djiboutian Francs. However, payment may be made in another currency if the obligation so denominated arises from an international contract or a foreign judgment.

###### Article 1544

In the absence of another designation by law, the contract or the judge, the place of payment of the monetary obligation is the creditor's domicile.

###### Article 1545

The judge may, taking into account the debtor's situation and in consideration of the creditor's needs, defer or schedule, within a limit of two years, the payment of sums due.

By special and reasoned decision, he may order that the sums corresponding to the deferred installments shall bear interest at a reduced rate at least equal to the legal rate, or that payments shall be imputed first to the principal.

He may make these measures conditional upon the debtor's performance of acts capable of facilitating or guaranteeing payment of the debt.

The judge's decision suspends enforcement proceedings that may have been initiated by the creditor. Interest increases or penalties provided for in case of delay are not incurred during the period fixed by the judge.

Any contrary stipulation is deemed unwritten.

The provisions of this article are not applicable to maintenance debts.

###### Subsection 3: Formal notice

###### Article 1546

Formal notice is the act by which either the creditor clearly indicates to his debtor that he does not intend to allow a contractual non-performance to continue, or the debtor enjoins his creditor not to prevent performance of the contract.

###### § 1. Formal notice to the debtor

###### Article 1547

The debtor is given formal notice to pay either by a summons or an act containing sufficient demand, or, if the contract so provides, by the mere falling due of the obligation.

###### Article 1548

Formal notice to pay a monetary obligation triggers default interest, at the legal rate. The creditor need not prove any loss.

###### Article 1549

Formal notice to deliver a thing places the risks on the debtor, if they are not already.

###### § 2. Formal notice to the creditor or "tender of payment"

###### Article 1550

Where the creditor, at the due date and without legitimate reason, refuses to receive the payment due to him or prevents it by his act, the debtor may give him formal notice to accept or permit its performance. This formal notice constitutes a tender of payment.

Formal notice to the creditor stops the running of interest due by the debtor and places the risks of the thing on the creditor, if they are not already. It is otherwise in case of gross negligence or fraud by the debtor.

Formal notice does not interrupt prescription.

###### Article 1551

If the obstruction has not ended within two months of the formal notice, the debtor may, where the obligation relates to a sum of money, deposit it at the registry of the Court of First Instance or, where the obligation relates to the delivery of a thing, sequester it with a professional custodian.

If sequestration of the thing is impossible or too costly, the judge may authorize its private sale or public auction. After deduction of the costs of sale, the price is deposited at the registry of the Court of First Instance.

Deposit or sequestration discharges the debtor from the time of their notification to the creditor.

###### Article 1552

Where the obligation relates to another object, for example an obligation to do, the debtor is discharged if the obstruction has not ceased within two months of the formal notice.

###### Article 1553

The costs of the formal notice and of the deposit or sequestration are borne by the creditor.

###### Subsection 4: Payment with subrogation

###### Article 1554

Subrogation takes place by operation of law alone for the benefit of one who, having a legitimate interest therein, pays when his payment discharges, towards the creditor, the one who is bound to the final burden of all or part of the debt.

###### Article 1555

Conventional subrogation is effected at the initiative of the creditor when the latter, receiving his payment from a third person, subrogates him in his rights against the debtor.

This subrogation must be express.

It must be granted at the same time as the payment, unless, in a prior act, the subrogor has manifested the intention that his co-contractor be subrogated to him upon payment. The concomitance of subrogation and payment may be proved by any means.

###### Article 1556

Subrogation also takes place when the debtor, borrowing a sum for the purpose of paying his debt, subrogates the lender in the rights of the creditor with the latter's participation. In this case, the subrogation must be express and the receipt given by the creditor must indicate the origin of the funds.

Subrogation may be granted without the participation of the creditor, but on condition that the debt is due or that the term is in favor of the debtor. It is then necessary that the loan deed and the receipt be executed before a notary, that in the loan deed it be declared that the sum was borrowed to make the payment, and that in the receipt it be declared that payment was made from the sums paid for this purpose by the new creditor.

###### Article 1557

Subrogation cannot harm the creditor when he has been paid only in part; in this case, he may exercise his rights, for what remains due to him, in preference to the one from whom he has received only partial payment. Subrogation transfers to its beneficiary, within the limit of what he has paid, the claim and its accessories, with the exception of rights exclusively attached to the person of the creditor.

However, the subrogee is entitled only to legal interest from a formal notice, if he has not agreed with the debtor on a new interest. These interests are secured by the security interests attached to the claim, within the limits, when they have been granted by third parties, of their initial commitments if they do not consent to bind themselves beyond.

###### Article 1558

The debtor may invoke subrogation as soon as he becomes aware of it, but it may only be enforced against him if it has been notified to him or if he has acknowledged it.

Subrogation may be enforced against third parties from the time of payment.

The debtor may raise against the subrogated creditor the defences inherent in the debt, such as nullity, the defence of non-performance, termination or set-off of related debts. He may also raise against him defences arising from his relationship with the subrogor before the subrogation became enforceable against him, such as the granting of a period of time, remission of debt or set-off of unrelated debts.

###### Section II: Set-off

###### Subsection 1: General rules

###### Article 1559

Set-off is the simultaneous extinction of reciprocal obligations between two persons. It takes effect, subject to being invoked, to the appropriate extent, on the date when its conditions are met.

###### Article 1560

Subject to the provisions set out in the following subsection, set-off only occurs between two obligations that are fungible, certain, liquidated and due.

Obligations for sums of money are fungible, even in different currencies, provided they are convertible, as are those which have as their object a quantity of things of the same kind.

###### Article 1561

Unseizable claims and obligations to restore a deposit, a loan for use or a thing of which the owner has been unjustly deprived may only be set off if the creditor consents thereto.

###### Article 1562

A period of grace does not prevent set-off.

###### Article 1563

If there are several debts that may be set off, the rules for appropriation of payments in articles 1392, 1394 and

1398 are transposable.

###### Article 1564

The debtor who has acknowledged without reservation the assignment of the claim may not raise against the assignee the set-off he could have raised against the assignor.

###### Article 1565

The surety may raise against the creditor the set-off that occurred between the latter and the principal debtor. The joint and several co-debtor may rely on the set-off that occurred between the creditor and one of his co-obligors to have the latter's divided share deducted from the total debt.

###### Article 1566

Set-off does not prejudice rights acquired by third parties.

###### Subsection 2: Special rules

###### Article 1567

Set-off may be ordered by the court even if one of the obligations, although certain, is not yet liquidated or due. Unless otherwise decided, the set-off then takes effect on the date of the decision.

###### Article 1568

The judge may not refuse the set-off of related debts solely on the ground that one of the obligations is not liquidated or due.

In that case, the set-off is deemed to have occurred on the day when the first of them became due.

In the same case, the acquisition of rights by a third party over one of the obligations does not prevent its debtor from raising the set-off.

###### Article 1569

The parties may freely agree to extinguish all reciprocal obligations, present or future, by set-off; this takes effect on the date of their agreement or, in the case of future obligations, on the date of their coexistence.

###### Section III: Merger

###### Article 1570

Merger results from the union of the capacities of creditor and debtor of the same obligation in the same person. It extinguishes the claim and its accessories, subject to rights acquired by or against third parties.

###### Article 1571

Where there is joint and several liability between several debtors or between several creditors, and the merger concerns only one of them, the extinction takes place, with regard to the others, only for his share.

Where the merger concerns a guaranteed obligation, the surety, even if joint and several, is released. Where the merger concerns the obligation of one of the sureties, the principal debtor is not released. The other joint and several sureties are released to the extent of the share of that surety.

###### Section IV: Remission of debt

###### Article 1572

Remission of debt is the contract by which the creditor releases the debtor from his obligation.

###### Article 1573

Remission of debt granted to one of the joint and several co-debtors releases the others to the extent of his share. Remission of debt made by only one of the joint and several creditors releases the debtor only for the share of that creditor.

###### Article 1574

Remission of debt granted to the principal debtor releases the sureties, even if joint and several.

Remission granted to one of the joint and several sureties does not release the principal debtor, but releases the others to the extent of his share.

What the creditor has received from a surety for the discharge of his suretyship must be applied to the debt and discharge the principal debtor proportionally. The other sureties remain liable only after deduction of the share of the released surety or of the value provided if it exceeds that share.

###### Section V: Impossibility of performance

###### Article 1575

Impossibility of performing the obligation releases the debtor to the appropriate extent when it results from a case of force majeure and is definitive, unless he has agreed to assume responsibility for it or has been previously given formal notice.

###### Article 1576

Where the impossibility of performance results from the loss of the thing owed, the debtor who has been given formal notice is nevertheless released if he proves that the loss would have occurred in the same way if the obligation had been performed. However, he is required to assign to his creditor the rights and actions attached to the thing.

##### Chapter V: Restitution

###### Article 1577

Restitution of a thing other than a sum of money takes place in kind or, where that is impossible, in value, assessed on the day of restitution.

###### Article 1578

The person who restores the thing is liable for the damage and deterioration that have reduced its value, unless he is in good faith and these are not due to his fault.

###### Article 1579

A person who, having received the thing in good faith, has sold it, is required to restore only the sale price. If he received it in bad faith, he owes its value on the day of restitution when it is greater than the price.

###### Article 1580

Restitution includes the fruits and the value of the enjoyment that the thing has provided.

The value of the enjoyment is assessed by the judge on the day he makes his decision.

Unless otherwise stipulated, restitution of fruits, if they are not found in kind, takes place according to a value assessed at the date of reimbursement, according to the state of the thing on the day of payment of the obligation.

###### Article 1581

Restitution owed to an unemancipated minor or to a protected adult is reduced in proportion to the benefit he derived from the annulled act.

###### Article 1582

In determining the amount of restitution, account is taken for the person who must make restitution, even if he is in bad faith, of the necessary and useful expenses for the preservation of the thing, up to the limit of the increase in value assessed on the day of restitution.

###### Article 1583

Restitution of a sum of money includes interest at the legal rate and taxes paid into the hands of the person who received it.

###### Article 1584

A person who received in bad faith owes the interest, the fruits he received or the value of the enjoyment from the time of payment. A person who received in good faith owes them only from the day of the claim.

###### Article 1585

Restitution of a service is made in value. This is assessed on the date on which it was provided.

Securities created for payment of the obligation are transferred by operation of law to the obligation to make restitution without, however, the surety being deprived of the benefit of the term.

#### Title V: On Civil Proof

###### Article 1586

The burden of proof lies with the person who claims recognition of a right or the performance of an obligation.

Conversely, the person who claims to be released must justify the fact that produced the extinction of the right asserted against him.

The judicial administration of evidence and disputes relating thereto are governed by the code of civil procedure.

Chapter I: The Admissibility of Methods of Proof

###### Article 1587

Except in cases where the law provides otherwise, proof may be provided by any means.

###### Article 1588

A juridical act concerning a sum or value exceeding the sum or value of 100,000 FD must be proved by writing under private or authentic signature.

It cannot be proved beyond or against a writing establishing a juridical act, even if the sum or value does not exceed this amount, except by another writing under private or authentic signature. A person whose claim exceeds the threshold mentioned in the first paragraph cannot be exempted from written proof by restricting his claim.

The same applies to a person whose claim, even if less than this amount, relates to the balance or part of a claim exceeding this amount.

###### Article 1589

The rules provided for in Article 1588 are subject to exception:

- in case of material or moral impossibility to obtain a writing,
- if it is customary not to establish a writing,
- or when the writing has been lost due to an external cause.

###### Article 1590

Writing may also be substituted by judicial admission, decisive oath, or a beginning of proof in writing corroborated by another means of proof.

###### Article 1591

Constitutes a beginning of proof in writing any written act that has emanated from the person against whom the claim is made, or from the person he represents, and that makes the alleged fact plausible. The statements made by a party during his personal appearance, his refusal to answer, or his absence from the appearance may be considered by the judge as equivalent to a beginning of proof in writing.

The mention of an authentic or privately signed writing in a public register is equivalent to a beginning of proof in writing.

##### Chapter II: Proof by Writing

###### Section I: General Provisions

###### Article 1592

No one may create a title for himself.

###### Article 1593

Proof of a juridical act may be preconstituted by a writing in authentic form or under private signature.

When a party does not know how to read, write, or sign, if it concerns an authentic act, the public officer shall have that person's fingerprints affixed to the act after having read it to him and asked if he consents to it. If it concerns an act under private signature, the person who does not know how to read, write, or sign first chooses a person of his choice who reads the act to him, then affixes his fingerprint on said act, and finally the person chosen signs the act as a witness.

###### Article 1594

A writing consists of a series of letters, characters, numbers, or any other signs or symbols endowed with intelligible meaning, whatever their medium.

###### Article 1595

Electronic writing has the same probative force as writing on paper, provided that the person from whom it emanates can be duly identified and that it is established and preserved under conditions likely to guarantee its integrity.

###### Article 1596

The signature necessary for the perfection of a juridical act identifies its author. It manifests his consent to the obligations arising from this act. When it is affixed by a public officer, it confers authenticity on the act.

When it is electronic, it consists in the use of a reliable identification process guaranteeing its link with the act to which it is attached.

###### Article 1597

In the absence of contrary provisions or agreements, the judge settles conflicts of proof in writing by determining by any means the most plausible title.

###### Section II: The Authentic Act

###### Article 1598

An authentic act is one that has been received, with the required formalities, by a public officer having the right to execute instruments in the place where the act was drawn up.

###### Article 1599

An act that is not authentic due to the incompetence or incapacity of the officer, or due to a defect of form, is valid as a writing under private signature if it has been signed by the parties.

###### Article 1600

The authentic act is conclusive until proven false as to what the public officer states he personally accomplished or observed.

Nevertheless, in case of complaints of principal forgery, the execution of the act alleged to be false shall be suspended by indictment; and, in case of incidental registration of falsity, the courts may, depending on the circumstances, provisionally suspend the execution of the act.

###### Section III: The Act Under Private Signature

###### Article 1601

An act under private signature, acknowledged by the party against whom it is opposed or legally held to be acknowledged with respect to him, is conclusive between those who subscribed to it and with respect to their heirs and successors in title.

###### Article 1602

A person against whom an act under private signature is opposed is obliged to formally acknowledge or disavow his writing or his signature.

His heirs or successors in title may likewise disavow the writing or signature of their predecessor, or may merely declare that they do not recognize the writing or signature of their predecessor. In these cases, verification of writing is ordered by the court.

###### Article 1603

An act under private signature evidencing a synallagmatic contract is proof only if it has been made in as many originals as there are parties having a distinct interest, unless the parties have agreed to deliver to a third party the single copy drawn up.

One original is sufficient for all persons having the same interest.

Each original must contain mention of the number of originals that have been made.

A person who has executed the contract, even partially, cannot raise the lack of plurality of originals or the mention of their number.

The requirement of a plurality of originals is deemed satisfied for contracts in electronic form when the act is established and preserved in accordance with Articles 1595 and 1596, second paragraph, and the process allows each party to have a copy on a durable medium or to have access to it.

###### Article 1604

An act under private signature by which one party undertakes to another to pay him a sum of money or to deliver to him a fungible good must include the signature of the person subscribing to this undertaking as well as the mention, written by himself, of the sum or quantity in words and figures. If the party declares that he does not know how or cannot sign, express mention is made in the act of his declaration, as well as of the reason preventing him from signing. The act is marked with his fingerprint.

###### Article 1605

When the sum expressed in the body of the act differs from that expressed by the handwritten mention, the act under private signature is proof for the sum written in words.

###### Article 1606

An act under private signature acquires certain date with respect to third parties only from the day it was registered, the day of death of a signatory, or the day its substance is recorded in an authentic act.

###### Section IV: Other Writings

###### Article 1607

The registers and documents that professionals must keep or establish have, against their author, the same probative force as writings under private signature; but the person who relies on them cannot divide the entries to retain only those that are favorable to him.

###### Article 1608

Domestic registers and papers do not constitute proof in favor of the person who wrote them. They constitute proof against that person:

1° In all cases where they formally state a payment received;

2° When they contain the express mention that the writing was made to compensate for the lack of instrument in favor of the person for whom they state an obligation.

###### Article 1609

The mention of a payment or other cause of discharge recorded by the creditor on an original instrument that has always remained in their possession constitutes a simple presumption of discharge of the debtor.

The same applies to the mention recorded on the duplicate of an instrument or a receipt, provided that this duplicate is in the hands of the debtor.

###### Section V: Copies of instruments

###### Article 1610

Copies, when the original instrument still exists, only constitute proof of what is contained in the instrument, the production of which may always be required.

When the original instrument no longer exists, a reliable copy has the same probative force as the original. Reliability is left to the judge's assessment. Nevertheless, an executory or authentic copy of an authentic writing is deemed reliable; the same applies to copies that were made by the authority of the magistrate, with the parties present or duly summoned, or to those that were made in the presence of the parties and with their mutual consent.

Copies that the judge does not consider reliable can only serve as a commencement of proof in writing.

Copies of copies may, depending on the circumstances, be considered as mere information.

###### Article 1611

The transcription of an act in public registers can only serve as a commencement of proof in writing; it will even be necessary for this:

1° That it be established that all the minutes of the notary, for the year in which the act appears to have been made, are lost, or that proof be provided that the loss of the minute of this act was caused by a particular accident;

2° That there exists a proper repertory of the notary, which establishes that the act was made on the same date. When, by means of the combination of these two circumstances, proof by witnesses is admitted, it will be necessary that those who were witnesses to the act, if they still exist, be heard.

###### Section VI: Acknowledging acts

###### Article 1612

The acknowledging act is the juridical act that establishes the existence of a prior act without modifying its substance. It constitutes acknowledgment of the pre-existing obligation. The acknowledging act does not dispense with the production of the original instrument, unless its content is specifically recited therein.

What it contains that is more or different from the original instrument has, in the absence of express intent of novation, no effect.

Nevertheless, if there were several conforming acknowledgments, supported by possession, and one of which is thirty years old, the creditor could be dispensed from producing the original instrument.

##### Chapter III: Proof by witnesses

###### Article 1613

The probative value of declarations made by a third party under the conditions of the code of civil procedure is left to the judge's assessment.

##### Chapter IV: Presumptions

###### Article 1614

Presumptions are consequences that the law or the magistrate draws from a known fact to an unknown fact.

###### Section I: Legal presumptions

###### Article 1615

Legal presumption is that which is attached by law to certain acts or certain facts, and which holds them as certain.

It exempts the person in whose favor it exists from providing proof thereof or shifts the object of proof. The presumption is said to be simple when the law reserves proof to the contrary; it is said to be irrefutable when it cannot be overturned.

###### Article 1616

The authority of res judicata only applies with respect to what was the subject of the judgment. It is necessary that the thing claimed be the same; that the claim be based on the same cause; that the claim be between the same parties, and made by them and against them in the same capacity.

###### Article 1617

Contracts concerning proof are valid when they relate to rights that the parties may freely dispose of.

Nevertheless, they cannot contradict irrefutable presumptions established by law, nor modify the faith attached to the admission or oath. Nor can they establish an irrefutable presumption in favor of one of the parties.

###### Section II: Judicial presumptions

###### Article 1618

Judicial presumptions are not established by law, but are left to the judge's assessment, who must only admit them if they are serious, precise and concordant, and only in cases where the law admits proof by any means.

##### Chapter V: Admission by a party

###### Article 1619

Admission is the declaration by which a person acknowledges as true a fact likely to produce legal consequences against them.

The admission that is opposed to a party is either extrajudicial or judicial.

###### Article 1620

Purely verbal extrajudicial admission is only received in cases where the law permits proof by any means.

Its probative value is left to the judge's assessment.

###### Article 1621

Judicial admission is the declaration made in court by the party or their specially mandated representative. It constitutes full proof against the person who made it.

It cannot be divided against its author.

It cannot be revoked, unless it is proven that it was the result of a mistake of fact; it cannot be revoked on the pretext of a mistake of law.

##### Chapter VI: The oath

###### Article 1622

The judicial oath is of two kinds:

1° That which a party refers to the other to make the judgment of the case depend on it: it is called decisory.

2° That which is referred ex officio by the judge to one or the other of the parties.

###### Section I: The decisory oath

###### Article 1623

The decisory oath may be referred in any kind of dispute.

###### Article 1624

It can only be referred concerning a fact personal to the party to whom it is referred.

###### Article 1625

It may be referred at any stage of the case, and even when there is no commencement of proof of the claim or the defense on which it is sought.

###### Article 1626

The oath may be referred back to the person who refers it, except when the fact that is its object is not that of both parties, but is purely personal to the person to whom the oath had been referred.

###### Article 1627

The person to whom the oath is referred, who refuses it or does not consent to refer it back to their adversary, or the adversary to whom it has been referred back and who refuses it, must fail in their claim or defense.

###### Article 1628

The oath only constitutes proof in favor of the person who referred it and their heirs and successors in title, or against them.

The oath referred by one of the joint and several creditors to the debtor only releases the latter for the share of that creditor.

The oath referred to the principal debtor also releases the sureties.

That referred to one of the joint and several debtors benefits the co-debtors.

That referred to the surety benefits the principal debtor.

In these last two cases, the oath of the joint and several co-debtor or of the surety only benefits the other co-debtors or the principal debtor when it has been referred concerning the debt, and not concerning the fact of joint and several liability or suretyship.

###### Section II: The oath referred ex officio

###### Article 1629

The judge may refer the oath to one of the parties, either to make the decision of the case depend on it, or only to determine the amount of the condemnation.

###### Article 1630

The judge may not defer the oath ex officio, either on the claim or on the defense raised against it, except under the following two conditions:

- 1. That the claim or defense is not fully justified;
- 2. That it is not totally devoid of proof.

Outside these two cases, the judge must either grant or reject the claim purely and simply.

###### Article 1631

The oath deferred ex officio by the judge to one of the parties cannot be referred by that party to the other.

###### Article 1632

The oath on the value of the thing claimed may only be deferred by the judge to the claimant when it is otherwise impossible to establish this value.

The judge must, even in this case, determine the sum up to which the claimant will be believed on his oath.

#### Titre VI: On the marriage contract and matrimonial property regimes

Chapitre Ier. General provisions

###### Article 1633

The law only governs the conjugal association, as to property, in the absence of special agreements, which the spouses may make as they see fit, provided they are not contrary either to good morals or to the provisions that follow.

###### Article 1634

The spouses, in the marriage act, indicate whether or not they have entered into a marriage contract.

They declare whether they opt for the matrimonial regime of the civil code. Mention of this is made in the marriage act.

When they opt for the civil code regime, they indicate the matrimonial regime they choose. In the absence of stipulations in this regard, the spouses will be subject to the legal community regime (article 1647 and following); and, with regard to third parties, the spouses will be deemed married under this common law regime whenever they have seized the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance or accept its jurisdiction when they are defendants, unless in the acts entered into with these third parties, they have declared having made a marriage contract falling under such regime as they will have indicated to them.

###### Article 1635

The spouses cannot derogate from the duties or rights that result for them from marriage or that are provided by law under the title of parental authority and guardianship.

###### Article 1636

The spouses cannot make any agreement or waiver the purpose of which would be to change the legal order of succession, without prejudice to inter vivos or testamentary gifts that may take place according to the forms and in the cases determined by this code.

###### Article 1637

The spouses can no longer stipulate in a general manner that their association will be governed by one of the customs, laws or local statutes that could govern the various parts of the Djiboutian territory, and which are repealed by this code.

###### Article 1638

All matrimonial agreements shall be drafted, before the marriage, by deed before a notary, in the presence and with the simultaneous consent of the future spouses and all persons who are parties to it or their representatives. Matrimonial agreements take effect on the day of the celebration of the marriage and cannot receive any change after this celebration.

Changes or counter-letters that could be made to these agreements before the celebration of the marriage must be recorded by deed before a notary and in the presence and with the simultaneous consent of all persons who were parties to it.

###### Article 1639

The notary issues to the parties, at the time of signing the contract, a certificate on unstamped paper and free of charge, stating his name and place of residence, the names, first names, qualifications and residences of the future spouses, as well as the date of the contract. This certificate indicates that it must be delivered to the civil registrar before the celebration of the marriage, which the notary also recalls orally to the future spouses.

In case of changes made to the initial deed, the notary drafts them following the original of the marriage contract; the notary may not issue engrossments or copies of the marriage contract without transcribing following them the changes or counter-letters that may have been made to it. In the absence of compliance with these formalities, the changes or counter-letters will have no effect with regard to third parties.

###### Article 1640

The minor capable of contracting marriage may consent to all agreements of which this contract is susceptible; and the agreements and gifts he has made therein are valid, provided he has been assisted, in the contract, by the persons whose consent is necessary for the validity of the marriage. The adult under guardianship or curatorship may enter into matrimonial agreements if he is assisted, in the contract, by his guardian or curator.

If matrimonial agreements have been entered into without this assistance, annulment may be requested by the incapable person or by the persons whose consent was required, but only for one year from the marriage.

###### Article 1641

Once the marriage has been celebrated, no change may be made to the matrimonial regime except by effect of a judgment:

1° When one of the spouses requests judicial separation of property due to disorder of affairs or misconduct of the spouse jeopardizing his interests;

2° When partial and temporary modifications to the rules setting the powers of the spouses are granted by the judge, such as when the other spouse is unable to express his will and a judicial authorization to act without the consent of the other spouse is granted (article 225 of this code), or when a judicial authorization to represent the other spouse has been decided (article 227 of this code), or in the case of transfer of powers over ordinary or reserved common property (article 1671 of this code), or transfer of powers over separate property (article 1674 of this code).

3° By effect of a notarial deed, if necessary approved by the judge, in the case of article 1642.

###### Article 1642

After two years of application of the matrimonial regime, the spouses may agree, in the interest of the family, to modify it, or even to change it entirely, by a notarial deed. Mention is made of the modification on the original of the modified marriage contract and, on pain of nullity, the notarial deed contains the liquidation of the modified matrimonial regime if it is necessary.

The persons who had been parties to the modified contract and the adult children of each spouse are personally informed of the contemplated modification; the creditors of the spouses are informed of it by the publication of a notice in a newspaper authorized to receive legal notices. Each of them may oppose the modification within a period of three months.

In case of opposition, the notarial deed is subject to approval by the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance of the domicile of the spouses. It is so obligatorily when one or the other of the spouses has minor children. The application and the decision of approval are published.

Non-opposing creditors, if fraud has been committed against their rights, may attack the change of matrimonial regime to have this deed declared unenforceable against them, on condition of establishing, if it is an act for valuable consideration, that the third party co-contractor had knowledge of the fraud. They must specify in what way the contested fraudulent acts are related to the change of matrimonial regime, which is not in itself indicative of fraud

###### Article 1643

The change of matrimonial regime takes effect between the parties on the date of the deed or judgment providing for it and, with respect to third parties, three months after mention thereof has been entered in the margin of the marriage certificate. However, even in the absence of such mention, the change is nonetheless enforceable against third parties if, in deeds executed with them, the spouses have declared that they have modified their matrimonial regime. When either spouse is subject to a legal protection measure under the conditions provided for in Title XII of Book I of this Code, the change or modification of the matrimonial regime is subject to the prior authorization of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance or of the family council if one has been established.

By way of exception, agreements entered into by spouses in divorce proceedings for the purpose of liquidating their matrimonial regime are governed by the provisions of this Code specific to the divorce proceedings initiated.

###### Article 1644

When a change to the matrimonial regime occurs by application of a foreign law governing the effects of the union, the spouses shall inform the persons who were parties to the marriage contract and each of their adult children and shall proceed, where applicable, with land registry publication. They shall have mention thereof entered in the margin of the marriage certificate.

###### Article 1645

The change of matrimonial regime takes effect between the parties from the date of the decision or deed providing for it and, with respect to third parties, three months after the publication formalities provided for in Article 1644 have been completed.

However, in the absence of completion of these formalities, the change of matrimonial regime is enforceable against third parties if, in deeds executed with them, the spouses have declared that they have modified their matrimonial regime.

##### Chapitre II: Of the community regime

###### Article 1646

The community, whether legal or conventional, begins on the day of the marriage contracted before the civil status officer: it cannot be stipulated that it will begin at another time.

###### Section I: Of the legal community

###### Article 1647

The community that is established in the absence of a contract, or by the simple declaration that one is marrying under the community regime, is subject to the rules explained in the following subsections.

###### Sous-section 1: Of what composes the community on the asset and liability sides

###### § 1. Of the assets of the community

###### Article 1648

The community is composed on the asset side of acquisitions made by the spouses together or separately during the marriage, and arising both from their personal industry and from savings made on the fruits and income of their separate property.

###### Article 1649

Any property, movable or immovable, is presumed to be a community acquisition unless it is proven to be separate property of one of the spouses by application of a provision of law. If the property is of a kind that does not bear in itself proof or indication of its origin, the separate ownership of the spouse, if contested, must be established in writing. In the absence of an inventory or other pre-existing proof, the judge may take into consideration all writings, including family documents, registers and domestic papers, as well as bank documents and invoices. He may even admit proof by testimony or presumption, if he finds that a spouse was materially or morally unable to obtain a written document.

###### Article 1650

Each spouse retains full ownership of his or her separate property. The community is only entitled to fruits received and not consumed. But compensation may be due to it, upon dissolution of the community, for fruits that the spouse has neglected to receive or has fraudulently consumed, without any claim, however, being admissible beyond the last five years.

###### Article 1651

Constitute separate property by their nature, even if they were acquired during the marriage, clothing and linens for the personal use of one of the spouses, actions for compensation for bodily or moral injury, non-transferable claims and pensions, and, more generally, all property of a personal nature and all rights exclusively attached to the person. Also constitute separate property by their nature, but subject to compensation if applicable, work instruments necessary for the profession of one of the spouses, unless they are accessories to a business or operation forming part of the community.

###### Article 1652

Remain separate property the assets of which the spouses had ownership or possession on the day of the celebration of the marriage, or which they acquire, during the marriage, by succession, gift or bequest. The liberality may stipulate that the property which is its object shall belong to the community. Property falls into the community, unless otherwise stipulated, when the liberality is made to both spouses jointly. Property relinquished or transferred by father, mother or other ascendant to one of the spouses, either to satisfy what is owed to him or her, or subject to paying the donor's debts to strangers, remains separate property, subject to compensation.

###### Article 1653

Constitute separate property, subject to compensation if applicable, property acquired as accessories to separate property as well as new securities and other increases relating to separate movable securities. Also constitute separate property, by effect of real subrogation, claims and indemnities that replace separate property, as well as property acquired through investment or reinvestment, in accordance with Articles 1678 and 1679.

###### Article 1654

Property acquired in exchange for property that belonged as separate property to one of the spouses is itself separate property, subject to compensation due to the community or by it, if there is a balance payment. However, if the balance payment charged to the community is greater than the value of the property transferred, the property acquired in exchange falls into the common mass, subject to compensation in favor of the transferor.

###### Article 1655

The acquisition made, by way of auction sale or otherwise, of a portion of property of which one of the spouses was an undivided owner, does not constitute an acquisition, except for compensation due to the community for the sum it may have provided.

###### § 2. Of the liabilities of the community

###### Article 1656

The community is composed on the liability side:

- definitively, of support owed by the spouses and debts contracted by them for the maintenance of the household and the education of the children, in accordance with Article 228;
- definitively or subject to compensation, as the case may be, of other debts arising during the community.

###### Article 1657

Debts for which the spouses were liable on the day of the celebration of their marriage, or with which the successions and liberalities that fall to them during the marriage are encumbered, remain their personal debts, both as to principal and as to arrears or interest.

###### Article 1658

The creditors of either spouse, in the case of Article 1657, may only pursue payment from the separate property and income of their debtor.

They may, however, also seize community property when the movables that belonged to their debtor on the day of the marriage or that fell to him or her by succession or liberality have been commingled in the common patrimony and can no longer be identified according to the rules of Article 1649.

###### Article 1659

Compensation is due to the community that has discharged the personal debt of a spouse.

###### Article 1660

Payment of debts for which each spouse is liable, for whatever cause, during the community, may always be pursued from common property, unless there has been fraud by the debtor spouse and bad faith by the creditor, subject to compensation due to the community if applicable.

###### Article 1661

The earnings and wages of a spouse may not be seized by the creditors of their spouse unless the obligation was contracted for the maintenance of the household or the education of the children, in accordance with Article 228.

###### Article 1662

Each spouse may only encumber their separate property and income by means of a surety or loan, unless these have been contracted with the express consent of the other spouse who, in that case, does not encumber their separate property.

###### Article 1663

The community which has paid a debt for which it could be sued under the preceding articles is nevertheless entitled to reimbursement whenever that obligation had been contracted in the personal interest of one of the spouses, such as for the acquisition, preservation or improvement of separate property.

###### Article 1664

The community is entitled to reimbursement, after deduction, where applicable, of the profit gained by it, when it has paid fines incurred by a spouse by reason of criminal offences, or the damages and costs to which the spouse was sentenced for civil delicts or quasi-delicts. It is similarly entitled to reimbursement if the debt it has paid was contracted by one of the spouses in disregard of the duties imposed by marriage.

###### Article 1665

When a debt has entered the community on account of only one spouse, it may not be pursued against the separate property of the other. If there is joint and several liability, the debt is deemed to enter the community on account of both spouses.

###### Sous-section 2: Administration of the community and separate property

###### Article 1666

Each spouse has the power to administer alone the community property and to dispose of it, subject to being liable for faults committed in their management. Acts performed without fraud by one spouse are binding on the other. The spouse who exercises a separate profession alone has the power to perform the acts of administration and disposition necessary for it. All subject to Articles 1667 to 1670.

###### Article 1667

The spouses may not, one without the other, dispose inter vivos gratuitously of community property. Nor may they, one without the other, apply any such property as security for the debt of a third party.

###### Article 1668

A bequest made by a spouse may not exceed their share in the community. If a spouse has bequeathed an item of the community, the legatee may only claim it in kind to the extent that the item, upon partition, falls into the lot of the testator's heirs; if the item does not fall into the lot of those heirs, the legatee has reimbursement of the total value of the bequeathed item, against the share in the community of the heirs of the testator spouse and against the personal property of the latter.

###### Article 1669

The spouses may not, one without the other, alienate or encumber with real rights the immovable property, business assets and undertakings belonging to the community, nor non-negotiable company rights and corporeal movables whose alienation is subject to publicity. They may not, without their spouse, collect the capital proceeds from such transactions. Likewise, they may not, one without the other, transfer community property into a fiduciary estate.

###### Article 1670

The spouses may not, one without the other, lease rural land or immovable property for commercial, industrial or artisanal use belonging to the community. Other leases on community property may be entered into by one spouse alone and are subject to the rules provided for leases entered into by the usufructuary.

###### Article 1671

If one of the spouses is, in a lasting manner, unable to express their will, or if their management of the community demonstrates incompetence or fraud, the other spouse may apply to the court to be substituted in the exercise of their powers. The provisions of Articles 1689 to 1692 are applicable to this application.

The spouse, thus authorized by the court, has the same powers as the spouse they replace would have had; they perform with court authorization the acts for which their consent would have been required had there been no substitution. The spouse deprived of their powers may subsequently apply to the court for their restoration, by establishing that their transfer to the other spouse is no longer justified.

###### Article 1672

If one of the spouses has exceeded their powers over community property, the other, unless they have ratified the act, may apply for its annulment. The action for nullity is open to the spouse for two years from the day on which they became aware of the act, but may never be brought more than two years after the dissolution of the community.

###### Article 1673

Each spouse has the administration and enjoyment of their separate property and may dispose of it freely.

###### Article 1674

If one of the spouses is, in a lasting manner, unable to express their will, or if they endanger the interests of the family, either by allowing their separate property to deteriorate or by dissipating or misappropriating the income derived from it, they may, at the request of their spouse, be divested of the rights of administration and enjoyment granted to them by Article 1673. The provisions of Articles 1689 to 1691 are applicable to this application.

Unless the appointment of a judicial administrator appears necessary, the judgment confers on the applicant spouse the power to administer the separate property of the divested spouse, and to collect the fruits thereof, which must be applied by them to the charges of the marriage and the surplus used for the benefit of the community. From the date of the application, the divested spouse may only dispose alone of the bare ownership of their property. They may subsequently apply to the court to be restored to their rights, if they establish that the causes which had justified the divestment no longer exist.

###### Article 1675

If, during the marriage, one of the spouses entrusts the administration of their separate property to the other, the rules of mandate are applicable. The mandatary spouse is, however, dispensed from accounting for the fruits, when the power of attorney does not expressly require it.

###### Article 1676

When one of the spouses takes over the management of the separate property of the other, with the latter's knowledge, and nevertheless without opposition on their part, they are deemed to have received a tacit mandate, covering acts of administration and enjoyment, but not acts of disposition. That spouse is liable for their management to the other as a mandatary. They are, however, accountable only for existing fruits; for those which they have neglected to collect or fraudulently consumed, they may only be held liable within the limit of the last five years.

If it is in disregard of established opposition that one of the spouses has interfered in the management of the separate property of the other, they are liable for all the consequences of their interference and accountable without limitation for all the fruits which they have collected, neglected to collect or consumed.

###### Article 1677

The community owes reimbursement to the owner spouse whenever it has benefited from separate property. This is the case, in particular, when it has collected separate funds or funds from the sale of separate property, without there having been investment or reinvestment thereof.

If a dispute arises, proof that the community has benefited from separate property may be adduced by all means, including testimony and presumptions.

###### Article 1678

Investment or reinvestment is deemed made with regard to a spouse whenever, upon an acquisition, they have declared that it was made with separate funds or funds from the alienation of separate property, and to serve as investment or reinvestment. In the absence of this declaration in the act, the investment or reinvestment takes place only by agreement of the spouses, and it produces its effects only in their mutual relations.

###### Article 1679

If the investment or reinvestment is made in anticipation, the property acquired is separate property, on the condition that the sums expected from the separate estate are paid to the community within five years from the date of the deed.

###### Article 1680

When the price and costs of acquisition exceed the sum that has been invested or reinvested, the community is entitled to reimbursement for the excess.

If, however, the contribution of the community is greater than that of the acquiring spouse, the acquired property falls into the community, except for the reimbursement owed to the spouse.

###### Article 1681

Whenever a sum is taken from the community, either to discharge the debts or personal obligations of one of the spouses, such as the price or part of the price of property that is separate property or the redemption of land services, or for the recovery, preservation or improvement of his or her personal property, and generally whenever one of the two spouses has derived a personal benefit from the community property, he or she owes reimbursement for it.

###### Article 1682

If the father and mother have jointly endowed the common child without expressing the portion for which they intended to contribute, they are deemed to have endowed each for one half, whether the dowry was provided or promised in community property, or whether it was in personal property of one of the two spouses. In the second case, the spouse whose personal property has been constituted as dowry has, against the property of the other, an action for indemnity for half of the said dowry, having regard to the value of the property given at the time of the endowment.

###### Article 1683

The dowry constituted to the common child, in community property, is borne by the community. It must be borne for one half by each spouse, upon dissolution of the community, unless one of them, in constituting it, has expressly declared that he or she would bear it entirely or for a portion greater than one half.

###### Article 1684

The guarantee of the dowry is owed by any person who constituted it; and its interest runs from the day of the marriage, even though there is a term for payment, if there is no stipulation to the contrary.

###### Sous-section 3: Of the dissolution of the community

###### § 1. Of the causes of dissolution and of separation of property

###### Article 1685

The community is dissolved:

1° by the death of one of the spouses;

2° by declared absence;

3° by divorce;

4° by legal separation;

5° by separation of property;

6° by change of matrimonial regime.

###### Article 1686

There can be no continuation of the community, notwithstanding any provision to the contrary. Either spouse may request, if appropriate, that, in their mutual relations, the effect of the dissolution be carried back to the date when they ceased to cohabit and to collaborate.

###### Article 1687

If, by the disorder of the affairs of one spouse, his or her mismanagement or misconduct, it appears that the maintenance of the community endangers the interests of the other spouse, the latter may pursue separation of property in court. Any separation, without the intervention of the judge, is null and void by operation of law.

###### Article 1688

Separation of property, although pronounced by the court, is null and void if the proceedings to liquidate the rights of the parties have not been commenced within three months of the judgment becoming final and if the final settlement has not occurred within one year of the opening of the liquidation proceedings.

This period of one year may be extended by the president of the Civil Chamber of the Court of First Instance ruling in summary proceedings.

###### Article 1689

The application and the judgment for separation of property must be published under the conditions and sanctions provided by the code of civil procedure.

The judgment that pronounces separation of property has retroactive effect, as to its effects, to the day of the application. Mention shall be made of the judgment in the margin of the marriage certificate as well as on the original of the marriage contract.

###### Article 1690

The creditors of one spouse may not request separation of property on his or her behalf.

###### Article 1691

When the action for separation of property has been initiated, the creditors may summon the spouses by lawyer to lawyer to communicate to them the application and supporting documents. They may even intervene in the proceedings for the preservation of their rights.

If the separation has been pronounced in fraud of their rights, they may challenge it by way of third-party opposition, under the conditions provided in the code of civil procedure.

###### Article 1692

The spouse who has obtained separation of property must contribute, in proportion to his or her means and those of his or her spouse, both to the expenses of the household and to those of the education of the children. He or she must bear these expenses entirely, if nothing remains to the other.

###### Article 1693

Separation of property pronounced by the court has the effect of placing the spouses under the regime of articles 1739 and following. The court, in pronouncing the separation, may order that one spouse pay his or her contribution into the hands of his or her spouse, who shall henceforth assume alone with respect to third parties the payment of all the obligations of the marriage.

###### Article 1694

The agreements made in application of article 293 are suspended, as to their effects, until the pronouncement of the divorce; they may not be executed, even in relations between spouses, until the judgment has become final. One of the spouses may request that the divorce judgment modify the agreement if the consequences of the divorce fixed by that judgment call into question the bases of the liquidation and partition.

###### § 2. Of the liquidation and partition of the community

###### Article 1695

The community dissolved, each of the spouses takes back those properties that had not entered the community, if they exist in kind, or the properties that have been substituted for them. There is then occasion for liquidation of the common mass, assets and liabilities.

###### Article 1696

There is established, in the name of each spouse, an account of the reimbursements that the community owes him or her and of the reimbursements that he or she owes to the community, according to the rules prescribed in the preceding sections.

###### Article 1697

The reimbursement is, in general, equal to the lesser of the two sums represented by the expenditure made and the profit remaining. It may not, however, be less than the expenditure made when it was necessary. It may not be less than the profit remaining, when the borrowed value has been used to acquire, preserve or improve a property that is found, on the day of the liquidation of the community, in the borrowing estate. If the property acquired, preserved or improved has been alienated before the liquidation, the profit is evaluated on the day of the alienation; if a new property has been substituted for the alienated property, the profit is evaluated on that new property.

###### Article 1698

If, balance made, the account shows a balance in favor of the community, the spouse brings back the amount to the common mass. If it shows a balance in favor of the spouse, the latter has the choice either to require payment or to withdraw common property up to the proper amount.

###### Article 1699

Withdrawals are made first on cash, then on movable property, and subsidiarily on immovable property of the community. The spouse who makes the withdrawal has the right to choose the movable and immovable property that he or she will withdraw. He or she may not, however, prejudice by his or her choice the rights that his or her spouse may have to request the maintenance of undivided ownership or the preferential allocation of certain properties. If the spouses wish to withdraw the same property, it is proceeded, unless demonstration of an abuse by the one who opposes the withdrawal of a particular property by the other, by drawing lots.

###### Article 1700

In case of insufficiency of the community, the withdrawals of each spouse are proportional to the amount of recompense due to them. However, if the insufficiency of the community is attributable to the fault of one of the spouses, the other spouse may exercise their withdrawals before them on all common property; they may exercise them subsidiarily on the separate property of the responsible spouse.

###### Article 1701

Recompense owed by the community or to the community bears interest by operation of law from the day of dissolution. However, when the recompense is equal to the remaining profit, interest runs from the day of liquidation.

###### Article 1702

Withdrawals from common property constitute a partition operation. They do not confer on the spouse exercising them any right to be preferred over the creditors of the community.

###### Article 1703

After all withdrawals have been executed from the mass, the surplus is divided in half between the spouses. If an immovable of the community is an annex to another immovable belonging separately to one of the spouses, or if it is contiguous to that immovable, the spouse who is the owner has the right to have it allocated to them by imputation on their share or by means of an equalizing payment, according to the value of the property on the day the allocation is requested.

###### Article 1704

The partition of the community, with respect to everything concerning its forms, the maintenance of joint ownership and preferential allocation, the sale by auction of property, the effects of partition, the warranty and equalizing payments, is subject to all the rules established under the title Of Successions for partitions among co-heirs.
